templates.title: Feed audience per month — the audience each payment was posted with
templates.subtopic: as-of lookups over a settings history, COALESCE precedence, ratio of counts per month

sections.scenario: A peer-to-peer payments app shows payments in a social feed. Each sender has a default audience setting — public, friends only, or private — which they can change at any time, and they can also choose a different audience on an individual payment before sending it. A privacy team wants to know, month by month, how payments were actually posted: what share went out public, friends-only and private. That depends on the setting in force when each payment was made, not on what the sender's setting is today.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, payments, public_share, friends_share, private_share, one row per month with at least one counted payment, ordered by month. month is the first day of the UTC month of created_at. A payment's audience is its audience_override when that is not NULL; otherwise it is the sender's default in force at created_at: the default_audience of the sender's latest feed_settings row with changed_at at or before created_at. {{initial_rule}} {{status_rule}} {{tie_rule}} payments counts the month's counted payments; each share is the number posted with that audience divided by payments, rounded to 4 decimal places.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A change at exactly the payment's created_at is in force for that payment. The sample has {{payments}} payments and {{changes}} setting changes; production has hundreds of millions of payments a month and far fewer setting changes.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical users, amounts, settings and schema. The three audience values and the override-wins rule are this exercise's model of a social payments feed; check current docs for any real product's settings. The report is aggregated per month and shows no individual's payments.
sections.criteria: One audience per payment with override precedence; the default as of created_at with an inclusive boundary, not the current setting; a deterministic tie-break on change_id (Very Hard); payments before any setting row kept with the initial default (Hard+); declined payments excluded (Hard+); later edits ignored (Very Hard); UTC months; numeric division and correct rounding; can discuss validity ranges and as-of joins at scale.

clarifications.q: The sender changed their default to private last week. Does that change how a payment from March was posted?
clarifications.a: No. A payment uses the default in force when it was created.

clarifications.q: A payment has an override and the sender's default differs.
clarifications.a: The override wins.

clarifications.q: A setting change and a payment have the same created_at and changed_at.
clarifications.a: The change is in force for that payment: at or before, inclusive.

clarifications.q: What if the sender has no setting row before the payment?
clarifications.a: {{initial_answer}}

clarifications.q: How are shares rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(count::numeric / payments, 4); the three shares of a month need not add up to exactly 1 after rounding.

hints: Resolve one audience per payment first; aggregate afterwards. The month and the shares are the easy part.

"The latest row at or before a time" is an as-of lookup: a correlated subquery with ORDER BY changed_at DESC … LIMIT 1, a LATERAL join, or validity ranges built with LEAD(changed_at) and a range join.
COALESCE(override, default_in_force, initial_default) expresses the precedence in one place.
followups: Build feed_settings validity ranges (valid_from, valid_to) once with LEAD. Which boundary is inclusive, and how do you make sure two rows at the same second never produce an empty or overlapping range?

At hundreds of millions of payments a month, which join strategy would you expect the engine to use for the as-of lookup, and how would you make it cheap (sorting, clustering, a range join, or a snapshot of settings per day)?
Users can later change the audience of a payment already in the feed. Model both "posted with" and "currently visible to" so both questions can be answered.
The privacy team now asks how many payments were posted public by senders who had switched to private within the previous 30 days. Write the definition precisely and the query outline.

rules.ask: Your lookup returns the sender's latest change. Latest as of when — today, or the moment of the payment? What does it return for a payment made before that change?
A setting changes at exactly 10:00:00 and a payment is created at 10:00:00. Which audience does your query give it, and which does the spec require?
What happens to a payment whose sender has no setting row before it? Does it disappear from payments?
How does your range handle the sender's newest row, whose valid_to is NULL, and two rows with the same changed_at?
How many index probes does this make at hundreds of millions of payments, and what index would make each one cheap?

templates.title: Cross-border corridors per week — speed to available and totals in each currency's units
templates.subtopic: latest row per key, ordered-set aggregates with FILTER, currency exponents as data, ISO weeks

sections.scenario: A wallet lets people send money abroad: the sender pays in one currency and the recipient receives another. A transfer is available when the recipient can use the money. Product and operations teams track each corridor (send currency to receive currency) weekly: how many transfers were sent, how quickly they became available, and how much money moved on each side. Currencies differ in their minor units — some have none, most have hundredths, a few have thousandths — so amounts are stored as integers in minor units, and each currency's exponent is kept as data.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, send_currency, receive_currency, transfers, available, median_minutes, sent_total, received_total, one row per week and corridor with at least one counted transfer, ordered by week_start, send_currency, receive_currency. week_start is the Monday (UTC) of the week of sent_at. {{log_rule}} {{status_rule}} transfers counts the corridor-week's counted transfers and available those that became available. median_minutes is the median (percentile_cont(0.5)) of the minutes from sent_at to available_at over the transfers that became available, NULL when none did. sent_total is the sum of send_amount_minor over counted transfers, and received_total the sum of receive_amount_minor over transfers that became available (0 when none did), each expressed in major units of its currency: the minor-unit sum divided by 10 to the currency's minor_exponent from currencies.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Never convert one currency into another: each total stays in its own currency. Keep money exact (numeric, not floating point). The sample has {{transfers}} transfers in {{rows_n}} rows; timestamps are recorded to the minute.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical corridors, amounts, delays and schema; the exchange rates implied by the amounts are made up. The exponents in currencies follow ISO 4217 for the codes used, but this exercise reads them from the table, never from code. How fast real cross-border transfers become available depends on the corridor and the product's own rules; check current docs.
sections.criteria: One current row per transfer (Very Hard); cancelled transfers excluded and pending ones counted only where specified (Hard+); Monday-based UTC weeks; the median with percentile_cont over available transfers only, NULL when none; each total scaled by its own currency's exponent from currencies, never converted, never by a hard-coded 100; numeric arithmetic; deterministic order; can discuss reporting-currency conversion, tail latency and late status rows.

clarifications.q: Which week does a transfer sent on Sunday at 23:58 UTC belong to?
clarifications.a: The week that started on the Monday before it. Weeks start Monday 00:00 UTC (date_trunc('week', …)).

clarifications.q: Does a pending transfer count?
clarifications.a: In transfers and sent_total only. It is not in available, the median or received_total.

clarifications.q: Can I divide every amount by 100?
clarifications.a: No. A currency with exponent 0 is already in whole units, and one with exponent 3 is in thousandths. Use currencies.

clarifications.q: Should the totals be rounded?
clarifications.a: They are exact: rounding to the currency's exponent changes nothing, but keep the division in numeric.

clarifications.q: Median or average?
clarifications.a: The median, with percentile_cont(0.5); with an even count it interpolates between the two middle values.

hints: Settle the grain first: exactly one current row per transfer. DISTINCT ON (transfer_id) … ORDER BY transfer_id, updated_at DESC is one way.
Join currencies twice — once for the send side, once for the receive side — and divide by power(10::numeric, minor_exponent).
percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) FILTER (WHERE available_at IS NOT NULL) and SUM(…) FILTER (…) keep each measure on its own population in one GROUP BY.
followups: Finance wants a single weekly total in one reporting currency. What would you need (rates, their timestamps, the rounding rule), and why must the conversion happen once per transfer rather than on the summed totals?
The median hides corridors where a few transfers wait days. Which other measure would you report, and how would you alert on a corridor-week that slows down?
The status log receives billions of rows. How would you maintain a current-state table incrementally, and what happens when an older status row arrives after a newer one?
A transfer is cancelled after the week was reported. How do the numbers change, and how would you make published weeks reproducible?

rules.ask: What does dividing by 100 do to an amount in a currency with no minor unit, and to one counted in thousandths?
Your speed measure is an average. What happens to it when one transfer in the week waits two days?
Where in your query could money pass through floating point, and why does that matter for a total someone will reconcile?
Two status rows of one transfer share an updated_at. What does your query keep, and how would you make it deterministic?
Which population does each of your columns cover, and how do you show that the median and received_total ignore pending transfers?

templates.title: Pay-later early payoff per purchase-amount band
templates.subtopic: range joins to a band table, LEFT JOIN for empty bands, per-plan aggregation before per-band, local dates

sections.scenario: A pay-later product lets a consumer split a purchase into instalments: in this exercise's rule (check current docs for any real product's terms), four instalments two weeks apart, the first at purchase, so the last falls due six weeks after the purchase. Consumers can also make extra payments at any time, and some pay the whole plan off before the final due date. A product team wants to see, by purchase-amount band, how many plans were paid off early and how often extra payments are used — to understand how the schedule fits purchases of different sizes. The analysis is about the product's design; it draws no conclusion about any person.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns band_id, label, plans, paid_off, paid_off_early, early_share, extra_payments, extra_cents, one row for every band in amount_bands, ordered by band_id. A plan belongs to the band with lower_cents <= purchase_cents and purchase_cents < upper_cents (a NULL upper_cents has no upper limit). {{status_rule}} A plan is paid off when its counted payments add up to purchase_cents (no plan in the sample is paid more), and paid off early when it is paid off and the date of its last counted payment is strictly before final_due_date. {{date_rule}} plans, paid_off and paid_off_early count the band's counted plans; early_share = paid_off_early / plans rounded to 4 decimal places, NULL when the band has no plans; extra_payments counts and extra_cents sums the counted payments with kind = 'extra' on the band's counted plans (0 when there are none).
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Aggregate each plan once before aggregating bands. The sample has {{plans}} plans and {{payments}} payments.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical plans, amounts, bands and schema. The schedule, the meaning of "early" and the band boundaries are this exercise's rules; check current docs for any real pay-later product. Late fees, refunds and rescheduling are out of scope. The report is aggregated per band and draws no legal, credit-worthiness or eligibility conclusion about any person.
sections.criteria: Range join with inclusive lower and exclusive upper bounds and an open top band; every band reported via LEFT JOIN with zeros and a NULL share; per-plan aggregation before per-band; paid off from the posted total; early strictly before the final due date; cancelled plans and reversed payments excluded (Hard+); the last payment's local date in the plan's time zone (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss immature cohorts, configurable bands and refunds without drawing conclusions about people.

clarifications.q: A plan of exactly 150.00 and bands 50–150 and 150–400.
clarifications.a: It belongs to 150–400: lower bounds are inclusive and upper bounds exclusive.

clarifications.q: The last payment was made on the final due date itself. Early?
clarifications.a: No. Strictly before the final due date.

clarifications.q: Which time zone decides the date of the last payment?
clarifications.a: {{date_answer}}

clarifications.q: A band has no plans. Do I still return it?
clarifications.a: Yes: zeros, and a NULL early_share.

clarifications.q: Does an extra payment on a plan that was never paid off count?
clarifications.a: Yes. extra_payments counts every counted extra payment on the band's counted plans.

hints: Build one row per plan with its paid total, its last payment time and its extra-payment count and cents, using a LEFT JOIN so plans with no counted payments survive.
Then LEFT JOIN that onto amount_bands with a range condition, so empty bands still appear, and count a column from the plan side.
Filter reversed payments in the join's source, not after the LEFT JOIN, or plans without payments vanish.
followups: Plans bought recently cannot be judged yet: their final due date is in the future. How would you report them honestly, and what bias appears if you include them?
Product proposes new band boundaries. How would you let analysts try several sets without changing the query, and how would you keep old reports reproducible?
A partial refund lowers what a consumer owes. How would you model it so "paid off" still means what the team expects?
At tens of millions of plans, how would you maintain this report daily rather than recomputing every plan?

rules.ask: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends. Which band does a purchase exactly on a boundary land in, and is it in two bands at once?
Which bands does your query return when no plan falls in the top band?
A plan's last payment is on the final due date. Is that early under this exercise's rule?
A consumer pays at 03:00 UTC on the due date and lives in Los Angeles. Which date did they pay on, and which date does your query use?
Where is your filter on reversed payments: in the join, or in a WHERE after the LEFT JOIN? What happens to a plan whose only payment was reversed?

templates.title: Mutual payers — pairs who paid each other in both directions within a window
templates.subtopic: directed-pair state, one pass after one sort, canonical pair keys

sections.scenario: In a peer-to-peer payments app, friends pay each other back: one covers dinner, the other pays them back a few days later. A product team designing "settle up" suggestions wants to know which pairs of people pay each other in both directions within a short window, when that first happened, and how often. The answer feeds aggregate product analysis; each pair only ever sees its own history.
sections.problem: Implement mutual_payers(payments, window_days, aliases=None). Each payment is (payment_id, sender, recipient, ts, status) with ts in whole seconds. Time order is (ts, payment_id): "earlier" means a smaller (ts, payment_id). {{order_rule}} {{alias_rule}} A counted payment from u to v at ts is reciprocating if there is an earlier counted payment from v to u at most window_days × 86 400 seconds before it. For every unordered pair with at least one reciprocating payment, return the key (a, b) with a < b and the value (first_id, gap, count): first_id is the payment_id of the pair's earliest reciprocating payment, gap is its ts minus the ts of the latest earlier counted payment in the other direction, and count is the number of reciprocating payments in the pair. Return a dict; pairs with none are left out. In this exercise window_days is {{window_days}}.
sections.constraints: Up to 250 000 payments among tens of thousands of users, and a few pairs with many thousands of payments each. Expected: O(n log n) for one sort, then O(1) per payment. Comparing every pair of payments is O(n²); comparing every payment of one direction with every payment of the other, per pair, is still far too slow for the busiest pairs.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical users, identifiers and payments. Pairs and counts are product analytics in aggregate; they say nothing about the relationship between two people and are never shown to anyone else.
sections.criteria: Counted payments filtered and recipients resolved before the walk; one sort by (ts, payment_id); latest time per directed pair in a dict; inclusive window; gap from the latest earlier opposite payment; first reciprocating payment by time, not by list position (Hard+); failed, refunded and self payments ignored (Hard+); identifiers resolved and unclaimed ones ignored (Very Hard); canonical sorted keys; O(n log n); credible discussion of incremental state, SQL formulation and privacy of pair-level data.

clarifications.q: Is a payment exactly window_days after the other direction's payment inside the window?
clarifications.a: Yes. At most window_days × 86 400 seconds, inclusive.

clarifications.q: Two payments in opposite directions at the same second.
clarifications.a: The one with the lower payment_id came first, so the other one is reciprocating, with a gap of 0.

clarifications.q: Which earlier payment does the gap measure from?
clarifications.a: The latest earlier counted payment in the other direction.

clarifications.q: Does the first payment of a pair ever count?
clarifications.a: No. A payment can only reciprocate one that came before it.

clarifications.q: Which way round is the key?
clarifications.a: The two users sorted as strings, whoever paid first.

hints: Sort the counted payments once by (ts, payment_id). Then walk them in order.
Keep a dict from a directed pair (sender, recipient) to the time of its latest payment so far. For a payment u → v, look up (v, u).
Normalise before you sort: drop what does not count and resolve recipients first, so the walk only sees real payments between two different users.
followups: The team wants "pairs who settled up": the second payment roughly equals the first. Define "roughly" in integer cents and say how the state you keep changes.
Run this daily over a payments table with billions of rows. What state do you carry from one day to the next, and how long must you keep it?
Express the same rule in SQL. Which join do you need, and why can it explode for the busiest pairs?
One user pays a hundred others and is paid back by most of them (a shared house). How would you summarise groups rather than pairs?

rules.ask: How many comparisons does your solution make for a pair with 8 000 payments each way, and how long is that in Python?
What is your sort key, and what happens to two payments in opposite directions at the same second?
Your key is unordered. How do you still know which direction a payment went, and which earlier payment to measure the gap from?
Bisect over each direction's times works. What does it cost compared with keeping the latest time per direction while walking in order?
An identifier changes hands: the phone number now belongs to someone else. Which owner should an old payment use, and what would the alias map need to record?

templates.title: Balance targets — the first date a wallet's balance reached each target
templates.subtopic: many queries over one history, sentinel answers, end-of-day aggregation

sections.scenario: A wallet app lets a user set savings goals and see milestones on their own balance history: "you first had 500.00 on 12 March". Behind the screen is a question asked many times over one history: for each amount, on which date did the balance first reach it? A user with years of activity may have hundreds of thousands of balance changes, and the milestone view asks for thousands of amounts at once. The data is the user's own activity, shown only to that user.
sections.problem: Implement balance_targets(opening_cents, events, targets, end_of_day=False). events lists (date, amount_cents) in the order they were applied, with date as 'YYYY-MM-DD' (dates never go backwards); the balance starts at opening_cents and each event adds its amount (negative for money out). {{opening_rule}} {{eod_rule}} For each target, in input order, return the date of the first event after which the balance was at least the target; 'opening' if opening_cents is already at least the target; or None if the balance never reached it. Return a list.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 events and 20 000 targets, many of them never reached. Expected: O(n + q log n). Replaying the history for each target is O(n·q), and stopping at the first hit does not help the targets that are never reached.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical amounts and dates. A milestone is a fact about the user's own history; it is not advice, and it says nothing about anyone's finances beyond what the user already sees.
sections.criteria: Running maximum recorded at its increases; bisect_left for the first value at least the target; inclusive comparison; answers in input order; 'opening' for targets met by the opening balance and None for unreached ones (Hard+); end-of-day closing balances only (Very Hard); O(n + q log n); credible discussion of incremental updates, restated history and multi-currency balances.

clarifications.q: The balance equals the target exactly. Reached?
clarifications.a: Yes: at least the target.

clarifications.q: The balance reached the target, then fell.
clarifications.a: It was still reached on that date.

clarifications.q: Two events on the same date.
clarifications.a: With end_of_day False, the balance after each event counts; with end_of_day True, only the balance after the date's last event counts.

clarifications.q: Can targets repeat or arrive unsorted?
clarifications.a: Yes. Answer each one in input order.

clarifications.q: What if events is empty?
clarifications.a: Every target above the opening balance is None.

hints: The first time the balance reached t is the first time the running maximum reached t, and the running maximum never decreases.
Record only the moments the running maximum rises (its value and the date). That list is sorted, so bisect_left finds the first value at least t.
With end_of_day, first reduce the history to each date's closing balance, then do the same.
followups: New events arrive every day. How would you keep the structure up to date, and which answers can change when one arrives?
A payment from last month is reversed and the history is restated. What breaks in your precomputed list, and how would you rebuild only what is needed?
The user wants the first date the balance stayed at or above a target for 30 consecutive days. How would you answer that for many targets?
Balances are held in several currencies. What does "reached 500" mean then, and what would you refuse to compute?

rules.ask: How many events does your loop read for a target that is never reached, and how many such targets are in the large test?
Which list are you searching, and why is it sorted even though the balance goes up and down?
Sorting the targets and sweeping once also works. What does it cost, and how do you return answers in input order?
Two events on the same date: one takes the balance to the target, the next spends it. What does each mode return?
Where could floating point enter, and why are integer minor units the right type for a balance?

templates.title: Settling a group's shared expenses — equal splits to the minor unit, net balances, largest creditor and largest debtor first
templates.subtopic: two priority queues over net balances, exact integer splits and conversion

sections.scenario: A group of friends shares costs on a trip: one person pays for dinner, another for the car, a third for tickets that only some of them used. The wallet's group feature records each expense with its payer and the people it was for, splits it equally, and at the end offers a "settle up" plan of transfers between members. The plan has to be reproducible: the same group must always get the same transfers, in the same order, so a member who sees the plan on two devices sees the same thing. Large community groups (clubs, shared houses over years) run to tens of thousands of members.
sections.problem:
Implement settle_group(members, expenses, repaid, currencies, home, remainder). members lists member ids in the order they joined. Each expense is (payer, amount, currency, participants): amount is in the currency's minor units, participants is a non-empty list of distinct members, and the payer may or may not be one of them.

  1. Split. An expense of A home minor units among k participants gives each a share of A // k, and the leftover A % k units go one each to the first A % k participants by the remainder rule. With remainder = 'listed' that is the order the expense lists them; with 'joined' it is the order of members. {{remainder_rule}}
  2. Balances. A member's net balance is what they paid minus the shares they owe. {{repaid_rule}} {{currency_rule}}
  3. Transfers. While some member has a positive balance and some member a negative one: take the creditor with the largest balance and the debtor with the most negative balance, each tie going to the member who joined first. The debtor pays the creditor min(creditor's balance, −debtor's balance), and both balances move by that amount.

Return the transfers as (from_member, to_member, amount) in the order they are made. Return [] when everyone is even.
sections.constraints: Up to 40 000 members and 64 000 expenses in the timing check, and almost every member ends with a non-zero balance. A scan of every member before each transfer is O(n²) and too slow. Something close to O(e + n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Members, amounts, rates and the remainder rules are hypothetical; this largest-first rule is this exercise's rule, so check current docs for how any real feature settles a group. The rule is not guaranteed to give the fewest transfers, and you must not optimise it away. Member ids are distinct. Balances always sum to zero, because splits add up exactly to each expense.
sections.criteria: Exact integer splits with the stated remainder rule; the payer's own share handled; net balances from expenses (and, at Hard, repayments that may overshoot); at Very Hard, each expense converted once with half-up rounding and its currency's own exponent before the split; the largest-first rule with join-order ties applied exactly, even when fewer transfers exist; an O(n log n) approach with two heaps (or another O(log n) structure); a termination and transfer-count argument; sensible answers on minimum transfers and incremental plans.

clarifications.q: Do I need the fewest possible transfers?
clarifications.a: No. The rule is largest creditor and largest debtor first. Finding the fewest transfers is a much harder problem; this exercise wants a fixed, explainable rule.

clarifications.q: Who gets the leftover cents of a split?
clarifications.a: The first A % k participants by the stated remainder rule, one unit each. Nobody gets a fraction of a minor unit.

clarifications.q: What if two creditors have the same balance?
clarifications.a: The one who joined the group first, the earlier one in members, is paid first. The same tie rule applies to debtors.

clarifications.q: Does the payer's own share count when they are a participant?
clarifications.a: Yes. They paid the whole amount and owe their share like everyone else, so their balance goes up by the amount minus their share.

clarifications.q: Is a member with a zero balance part of any transfer?
clarifications.a: Never.

hints: First compute every net balance in one pass over the expenses (and repayments). This part is linear.
Each transfer clears at least one of its two members, so there are at most n − 1 transfers. The cost is in finding the two largest each time.
Keep creditors and debtors in two heaps keyed by (−balance, join index) and (balance, join index). Pop one from each, transfer, and push back whichever still has a balance.
followups: Prove that the loop ends, and bound the number of transfers it makes.
The group wants fewer transfers. Show a group where the largest-first rule makes more transfers than necessary, and say why the fewest-transfers problem is hard in general.
Members can opt out of paying certain people directly (they never transfer to each other). How does that change the problem?

Expenses keep arriving after a plan was shown, and some transfers were already paid. How would you keep a plan up to date without recomputing it from scratch, and what must stay stable for the members?

rules.ask: With 40 000 members and about 40 000 transfers, how many balance comparisons does your loop make?
You sort after every transfer. What does that cost in total, and which structure would let you change two balances cheaply?
After a transfer, which of the two members do you push back, and how do you keep the join-order tie rule in the heap key?
Where does a fraction of a minor unit appear in your code, and how do you make the shares add up exactly to the expense?
The rule asks for largest first, not the fewest. What would it take to find the fewest, and why is it expensive?

templates.title: Lowest balance after back-dated activity — the wallet's low point as late events arrive
templates.subtopic: (sum, lowest prefix) per node, point updates for late and corrected events

sections.scenario: A wallet's activity does not always arrive in the order it happened. A bank transfer is dated the day it was initiated but confirmed days later; an offline card payment is forwarded hours after it was made; a payment from another currency is posted at the time of the original request. Each late event is inserted into the user's history at its own time, which changes every running balance after it. The user's own activity view shows the lowest balance the wallet reached and when, so the user can see whether it ever dipped below what they expected, and it must be right after every arrival, not only at the end of the day.
sections.problem: Implement lowest_balance(opening, arrivals). opening is the balance before any event, in minor units. arrivals lists events in the order they reached the wallet, each (event_id, t, amount): t is the integer minute the event took effect, and amount is a signed number of minor units. The history is every event that has arrived so far, ordered by t. {{tie_rule}} The running balance after an event is opening plus the amounts of every event up to and including it in history order. After each arrival, report (lowest, t): the lowest running balance over the whole history as it then stands, and the t of the earliest event in history order where that balance is reached. The opening balance on its own is not an event and is never the answer. {{correction_rule}} Return one tuple per arrival.
sections.constraints: Up to 80 000 arrivals in the timing check, 40% of them dated at a random earlier minute. Recomputing the running balances after each arrival is O(n) per arrival and O(n²) in total, and so is recomputing only from the inserted position on, because late events land early. Something close to O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Event ids, times and amounts are hypothetical. The balance may go below zero in this exercise; how any real wallet handles a negative balance is not part of it, so check current docs. Your function receives every arrival at once, but each answer must reflect only the arrivals up to that point.
sections.criteria: History ordered by time with arrival-order ties; running balances that include every earlier event after each insertion; the opening balance excluded; the earliest event on a tie; at Very Hard, corrections that rewrite an event in place and zero amounts that keep the slot; a segment tree (or equivalent) storing total and lowest prefix per node with O(log n) updates; a correct combine and tie argument; sensible answers on online insertion, range queries and multi-currency balances.

clarifications.q: After one arrival, what is the answer?
clarifications.a: That event's running balance, opening + amount, and its t. The opening balance alone is not a candidate.

clarifications.q: Two events reach the same lowest balance. Which t do I report?
clarifications.a: The earlier one in history order.

clarifications.q: Where does a back-dated event go when other events share its minute?
clarifications.a: After the events of that minute that arrived before it, so ties are always ordered by arrival.

clarifications.q: Do I know the final history in advance?
clarifications.a: Yes, the whole arrival list is an argument. You may preprocess it, but each reported answer must ignore events that have not arrived yet.

clarifications.q: Can amounts be zero or negative?
clarifications.a: Both. A debit is negative; a cancelled event (at Very Hard) has amount 0 and still occupies its place.

hints: Running balances are prefix sums in history order. The lowest running balance is the minimum prefix sum, plus opening.
For a block of events, keep two numbers: its total and its lowest prefix sum. Two adjacent blocks combine as total = L.total + R.total and low = min(L.low, L.total + R.low).

Since every event's final place in history is known in advance, give each event a slot in a fixed array of positions and build a segment tree over it. An arrival fills (or, for a correction, rewrites) one slot and updates its path to the root; empty slots are total 0 with a low of +∞. Keep the position of the low in each node, preferring the left on ties.
followups: Events now arrive one at a time and the final history is not known in advance. Which structure would you use instead of fixed slots?
The view also wants the lowest balance within a chosen date range. What does your tree need to answer that, and at what cost?
A user has ten years of history and the view changes for a back-dated event from three years ago. What would you store to avoid touching the whole history, and what would you show the user?
Balances are held in several currencies. What does "lowest balance" mean then, and what would you refuse to compute?

rules.ask: A late event lands near the start of an 80 000-event history. How many balances does your code touch for that one arrival?
What does each node store, and how do you combine a left and a right node so that the earliest low wins a tie?
Insertion is cheap with bisect. What about the balances after the insertion point?
What is the cost per arrival with your block size, and how does it compare with a tree at 80 000 events?
Your tree is online. What does each node keep about its subtree so the low can be read at the root?

templates.title: Debug the multi-currency wallet statement
templates.subtopic: minor-unit exponents, one rounding, reversals, local months, funding fallbacks

sections.scenario: Each month a wallet user can open a statement of their own payments: what they sent and received, converted to their home currency, and how their sent payments were funded. Support has passed on complaints about it. A user paid in yen sees a received amount a hundred times too small, and one paid in dinars sees it ten times too large. A user whose home currency is pounds finds a euro payment one penny off the converted amount shown when it arrived. A payment that was reversed shows in the statement, and so does its reversal, so both totals look inflated. A user in California sees a payment made on the evening of 30 September in October's statement. A payment that fell back to a card after the balance was declined shows in both "from balance" and "from linked", so the two add up to more than was sent. The statement code below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix monthly_statement(entries, month, offset_minutes, home, currencies, rates) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Currencies. currencies[code] is the currency's minor-unit exponent: 0, 2 or 3 decimal places. rates[code] = (num, den) means one major unit of code is worth num / den US dollars, and rates['USD'] is (1, 1).
  2. Conversion. An entry of amount minor units of code is converted to home minor units once, at the cross rate, as amount × num_code × den_home × 10^e_home / (den_code × num_home × 10^e_code), rounded half up. Nothing is rounded before that, and the statement adds the converted entries without further rounding.
  3. Entries. Each entry is a dict {"id", "ts", "kind", "currency", "amount", "reverses", "funding"}. ts is an ISO 8601 time in UTC. kind is "sent", "received" or "reversal". amount is positive. A reversal's reverses is the id of the payment it reverses. A sent payment's funding lists the attempts in order as (source, outcome), with source one of "balance", "bank", "card" and outcome "declined" or "used"; exactly one attempt is used.
  4. Month. An entry belongs to the statement when its time, moved to the user's fixed UTC offset offset_minutes (positive east of UTC), falls in month ("YYYY-MM").
  5. Reversals. A payment that has a reversal anywhere in entries, in this month or another, counts in neither total and adds 1 to reversed if the payment itself is in the month. Reversal entries never count in anything.
  6. Output. {"sent", "received", "net", "from_balance", "from_linked", "reversed"}: the converted totals of the month's sent and received payments that were not reversed, received − sent, the part of sent whose used source was the balance and the part whose used source was a bank or card, and the count of reversed payments.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. All arithmetic stays in integers. Up to 100 000 entries, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Rates, offsets, amounts and the reversal rule are hypothetical and this exercise's rules; check current docs for how any real statement converts currencies or shows reversals. Offsets are fixed, with no daylight-saving changes. The entries are the user's own, shown only to that user.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its user-facing symptom; each currency's own exponent; a single cross-rate conversion rounded half up once; reversed payments excluded and counted whatever month their reversal falls in, reversal entries never counted; local months computed by converting to the user's offset; only the used funding attempt counted; integer arithmetic throughout; minimal fixes with a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Should a payment be converted to US dollars first, then to the home currency?
clarifications.a: No. The rates are quoted against US dollars, but the conversion uses one cross rate and rounds once.

clarifications.q: How many decimal places does a currency have?
clarifications.a: Whatever currencies says: 0, 2 or 3. Never assume 2.

clarifications.q: A payment in September was reversed in October. Which statement shows it?
clarifications.a: Neither September's totals nor October's include it. September counts it as reversed, and the reversal entry itself is never counted.

clarifications.q: Which month does 02:00 UTC on 1 October belong to for a user at −300?
clarifications.a: 30 September, 21:00 local time, so September.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Convert 1 000 yen to US cents by hand with a rate of (67, 10000), then call the helper.
Take a euro amount and convert it to pounds twice: once at the cross rate, rounded once, and once through rounded US cents. Find an amount where the two differ.
Read the date helper: does it convert the time to the user's offset, or relabel it?
For a sent payment funded after a declined attempt, count how many times its amount is added.
followups: Rates change during the month. Which rate should each entry use, and what would you store on the entry so the statement can always be reproduced?
A reversal arrives after the statement for that month was already shown. Do you restate the old statement, and how does the user learn what changed?
The user moves from UTC−5 to UTC+1. Which months could change, and what offset would you store with each entry?
A user's statement should match the sum of their converted payment notifications to the minor unit. List the reasons it might not, and which rule in this specification prevents each.

rules.ask: Where does your code assume two decimal places? Give one currency for which that is wrong in each direction.
Show an amount where converting through rounded US cents and converting once at the cross rate disagree.
What is the difference between relabelling a time with a new offset and converting it to that offset? Which one does a statement need?
The reversal falls in the next month. Which statement shows the original payment, and what does the user see in each month?
Which rounding does your code apply to an amount that converts to exactly half a minor unit, and where is that stated?

templates.title: Funding attempts as events — each source tried, declined or used, the fallback chosen, and what the user was shown
templates.subtopic: attempt-level events, correlation ids, client and server events joined, funnel-safe analytics

clients: web, the apps and checkout buttons on merchant sites

sections.scenario: When a user sends a payment, the wallet tries a funding source: the balance, a linked bank account or a linked card. If that source is declined (insufficient balance, a bank that does not respond in time, a card that has expired), the wallet may fall back to another source, up to {{max_attempts}} attempts per payment, by this exercise's rule. The user sees a sequence of screens: the source chosen, sometimes a message that a fallback was used, sometimes a prompt to pick another source. About {{daily_payments}} payments a day come from {{clients}}. Product and support teams want to know how often each source is declined, which fallbacks succeed, how long users wait, and what they were shown, without ever logging card or account numbers. Client events can arrive up to {{late_hours}} hours late.
sections.problem: Design the events and the pipeline that turn funding attempts into analytics. Cover the event model (payment, attempt, user-facing screen), the identifiers that tie an attempt to its payment and to the screens shown, how server outcomes and client screens are joined when they arrive out of order or late, how a decline reason is recorded without sensitive detail, the tables analysts use (attempt-level facts and payment-level outcomes), and how the numbers reconcile with the payments that actually completed.
sections.constraints: No card numbers, bank account numbers, or other credentials appear anywhere in the analytics events, only an opaque reference to the linked source and its kind. Each payment has at most {{max_attempts}} attempts, and the attempt order must be recoverable. Retries of an event from the client must not double count. Payment-level counts must equal the count of completed payments in the payment system of record for every day. Reports must be re-runnable for any past day after late events arrive.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, attempt limits and lateness are hypothetical. Decline reasons come from a fixed list of coarse categories (insufficient balance, issuer declined, timeout, source expired, risk hold) chosen for this exercise; risk decisions are represented only as "a score you are given" and a hold, never their inputs. The fallback rule is this exercise's, so check current docs for how any real wallet chooses a source.
sections.criteria: A clear event model separating payments, attempts and screens; ids that preserve attempt order and tie screens to payments; server outcomes authoritative for money and client events for experience; no credentials in analytics, coarse decline categories, risk only as a given score and hold; deduplication of client retries; late events with re-runnable partitions; attempt-level and payment-level tables with explicit denominators; daily reconciliation with completed payments; sensible handling of new source kinds and per-user features kept apart from aggregates.

clarifications.q: Who decides the fallback, the client or the server?
clarifications.a: The server chooses and records it; the client shows a screen. Your model must keep both and say which is authoritative for what.

clarifications.q: Is a declined attempt that the user never saw still an event?
clarifications.a: Yes. Silent fallbacks are exactly what the product team wants to measure.

clarifications.q: Can a user cancel during a fallback prompt?
clarifications.a: Yes. That payment ends without completing, and its attempts still count.

clarifications.q: May we log the last four digits of a card?
clarifications.a: Not in analytics. Use an opaque per-source reference and its kind; the user's own app can show its own details from the system of record.

clarifications.q: How late can a client screen event arrive?
clarifications.a: Up to {{late_hours}} hours, for example from a phone that went offline.

hints: Give every payment an id at the server, every attempt an (payment_id, attempt_no), and every screen a client event id that carries the payment id.
Treat the server's attempt outcomes as the source of truth for money, and client screens as the source of truth for what the user saw.
Build payment-level outcomes from attempts, then left-join screens with an allowed lateness, and reconcile daily counts with the payment system of record.
followups: Analysts report that "fallback success" doubled overnight. List the pipeline causes you would check before believing it.
A new funding source kind is added next quarter. What has to change in the events, the tables and the reports?
The team wants per-user "you often fall back to your card" tips. What data does that need, who may see it, and how would you keep it out of the aggregate tables?
At {{daily_payments}} payments a day, late client events keep rewriting old partitions. How would you bound that cost and tell analysts when a day is final?

rules.ask: Which table would that field land in, who can read it, and what opaque reference would replace it?
Which question needs that identifier, and could the payment id answer it instead?
Where exactly is a retried client event dropped, and what key do you use?
A screen event arrives {{late_hours}} hours late for a payment already reported. What changes in yesterday's numbers, and who notices?
What is the denominator of your success rate: attempts, payments or users? Show how the choice changes the number.

incidents: A client release resends every funding screen event when the app resumes, for two days, so "fallback notices shown" doubles while server attempts do not.
One decline path starts copying the issuer's raw response, including a masked card number, into the decline detail field for six hours.

templates.title: Exchange-rate quotes shown and used — quotes with expiry, conversions accepted, and proof that the rate applied is the rate the user saw
templates.subtopic: quote records, expiry, quote-to-conversion binding, audit and reconciliation

sections.scenario: Before a user sends money across currencies, the wallet shows a quote: the amount the recipient will get, the rate including the conversion fee, and how long the quote holds ({{quote_ttl}} in this exercise). If the user accepts in time, the conversion must use exactly that rate; if the quote expires, a new one is shown. Users and regulators can ask later what rate was shown and applied. About {{daily_quotes}} quotes a day are shown across {{currency_pairs}} currency pairs, and most are never accepted. Currencies have 0, 2 or 3 decimal places, and amounts are integer minor units.
sections.problem: Design how quotes, acceptances and conversions are recorded and proven. Cover the quote record (pair, rate, fee, amounts, issued and expiry times, the rate source version), how an acceptance is bound to one quote and checked against its expiry, the conversion record and its link to the quote, the stated rounding rule applied once, retention of quotes nobody accepted, how you prove for any conversion that the applied rate equals the rate shown, and the reconciliation that finds conversions without a valid quote.
sections.constraints: A quote is immutable once shown. An acceptance after expiry must never use the expired rate. A quote can be accepted at most once, even if the client retries. Every conversion must be traceable to the quote shown, for {{audit_years}} years. Rounding happens once, by a stated rule, with each currency's exponent taken from data. Unaccepted quotes are numerous and may be kept for a shorter time than accepted ones.
sections.assumptions: Rates, fees, the quote lifetime and retention periods are hypothetical and this exercise's rules; check current docs for how any real service quotes or discloses conversion rates. The base rates come from an upstream feed that publishes versioned rate sets.
sections.criteria: An immutable quote record with id, pair, base rate, fee, amounts, issue and expiry times and rate-set version; acceptance bound to one quote with an atomic expiry and single-use check on server time; conversions carrying the quote id and the inputs to a single, versioned rounding with per-currency exponents; a reconciliation that finds conversions without a valid quote or with mismatched amounts; differentiated retention with audit for accepted quotes; a credible incident plan for a bad upstream rate.

clarifications.q: Whose clock decides whether a quote has expired?
clarifications.a: The server's at acceptance. The client's timer is a display only.

clarifications.q: Can the same quote be shown on two devices?
clarifications.a: It can be fetched again by its id, but it is one quote, and it can be accepted only once.

clarifications.q: What do we need to keep for quotes nobody accepted?
clarifications.a: Enough for aggregate analysis of quotes shown and expired; you decide how long and at what grain, and say why.

clarifications.q: Is the fee part of the rate?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the quoted rate includes the fee, and the quote records the base rate and the fee separately so both can be shown.

clarifications.q: Where does rounding happen?
clarifications.a: Once, when the recipient amount is computed from the sender amount, half up in this exercise, using the destination currency's exponent.

hints: Make the quote a first-class immutable record with its own id, and make the conversion carry that id.
Check expiry and single use in one atomic step at acceptance (for example, a conditional update from open to accepted with now < expires_at).
Store the inputs to the amount (sender amount, rate, exponents, rounding rule version), so any conversion can be recomputed and compared.
followups: The upstream rate feed publishes a wrong rate for one pair for five minutes. Which quotes and conversions are affected, and how do you find them?
A user says they were charged a different rate than they saw. Walk through the evidence you would produce.
Product wants to show a quote that holds for {{quote_ttl}} even when the market moves quickly. What risk does the business carry, and what data would you build to measure it?
At {{daily_quotes}} quotes a day, the quote store dominates storage. How do you tier and expire it without breaking the audit trail for accepted ones?

rules.ask: The cache loses the quote before the user accepts. What does the user see, and could the conversion ever use a different rate?
How is the rate stored, and which exact computation turns a sender amount into recipient minor units?
Two acceptances of the same quote arrive 50 ms apart from two devices. Show the step that lets exactly one win.
The acceptance arrives one second after expiry because the network was slow. What happens, and what does the user see?
How would you prove to an auditor, {{audit_years}} years later, that a conversion used the shown rate?

incidents: The upstream feed publishes a rate set in which one pair's rate is off by a factor of 100 for five minutes, and quotes with a {{quote_ttl}} lifetime are issued from it.
A deploy makes the acceptance check compare expiry with the time the client reports, and for one day acceptances up to a minute after expiry succeed.

templates.title: The wallet as data — accounts, linked banks and cards, the preferred funding source, balances in several currencies, holds, and what funded each payment
templates.subtopic: funding instruments and links over time, preference history, per-currency balances from movements, holds, funding legs per payment

sections.scenario: A consumer wallet has about {{accounts}} accounts. A user links bank accounts and cards, can hold a balance in up to {{currencies}} currencies, and picks a preferred funding source. About {{payments_per_day}} payments a day leave wallets, to friends and to merchants at checkout. In this exercise's funding rule (check current docs), a payment uses the balance in the payment's currency first, then the preferred funding source for the rest, and, if that source is declined, a fallback the user approved; so one payment can be funded from two or three sources. Some incoming money is placed on hold for up to {{hold_days}} days before it can be spent, when a review process you are given asks for it. Users ask "what paid for this?" and "why can't I use this money yet?"; support asks "which source was preferred on that date?"; analytics wants the funding mix per day and currency, in aggregate.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the wallet. Cover users and accounts; funding instruments (banks and cards) and the user's links to them over time (linked, verified, removed); the preferred funding source as a history; balances per currency, derived from append-only balance movements, with available and held amounts; holds and their release; conversions between the user's own currency balances; and the funding of each payment as one or more funding legs that add up to the payment. Show how you answer: what funded payment X; the available and held balance in currency C at time T; the preferred source on date D; and the daily funding mix per currency in aggregate.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer minor units; each currency's exponent (0, 2 or 3) comes from a currency reference table and is never assumed. A conversion is recorded once, with the rate applied, and rounded once by this exercise's rule (half away from zero, to the target currency's minor unit). No balance is stored as the only truth: every change is a movement, and a stored balance is a derived, rebuildable figure. Card and bank numbers never enter the model; instruments are tokens, with a short display suffix shown only to the instrument's owner. The available balance never goes below zero (this exercise's rule). Analytics read aggregates; a user sees only their own activity.
sections.assumptions: Account counts, volumes, currency counts and hold lengths are hypothetical. Card and bank network messaging is out of scope: a decline arrives as an event with a reason code. Fees are out of scope unless you add them. Any risk score comes from another system and is only referenced.
sections.criteria: Instruments as tokens kept apart from the user's links to them, both with validity intervals; preference as a history; per-currency balances derived from append-only movements with available and held parts; holds as placed and released movements; conversions recorded once with the rate and a single rounding; funding legs that reconcile exactly to each payment, with refunds tied to the legs they reverse; exponents taken from reference data; no card or bank numbers; concurrency on the available balance handled on the write path; aggregate funding mix by leg amount; incidents explained by the model and repaired without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Is the balance one number per user?
clarifications.a: No. A user can hold a balance in several currencies; each currency is its own balance with an available part and a held part.

clarifications.q: Does a payment in euros spend the dollar balance?
clarifications.a: Not automatically in this exercise. The euro balance is used first; the rest comes from the preferred source, converted if needed at a quoted rate that is recorded with the payment.

clarifications.q: Can a removed card come back?
clarifications.a: If the user links the same card again, it is a new link to the same instrument token in this exercise; the old link keeps its history.

clarifications.q: Who places a hold and for how long?
clarifications.a: A review process you are given places it, for up to {{hold_days}} days here. It is released early or at the end, and the release is an event of its own.

clarifications.q: Where does a refund of a payment go?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, back to the sources that funded it, in the reverse order they were used. Say how your model records which legs a refund reverses.

hints: Separate the instrument (a bank or card, as a token) from the user's link to it, and keep each with its own validity interval.
A balance is a sum of movements per account and currency; available and held are two sums. A hold is a pair of movements (placed, released), not a flag.
Funding legs per payment: (payment, leg number, source kind, instrument or balance currency, amount in the source's currency, amount in the payment's currency, conversion reference).
followups: Write the query for the available and held balance in one currency at time T. What snapshot or index keeps it fast for an account with years of history?
A payment of 50.00 EUR used 18.40 EUR of balance and the rest from a card billed in USD. Show the rows written, including the conversion, and the check that proves the legs add up to the payment.
The user removes the preferred card on the 3rd and picks a bank account on the 10th. What does "preferred source on the 5th" return, and what funded a payment on the 5th?
At {{payments_per_day}} payments a day, which tables are facts, at what grain, and how do you build the daily funding mix per currency without reading every movement?
Two payments start at the same moment against one available balance that covers only one of them. How do the model and the write path keep the balance from going negative?

rules.ask: Support asks what the user's available euro balance was at 14:05 last Tuesday; a hold was placed at 14:00 and released at 14:30. With one balance column, how do you answer?
Card numbers never enter this model. What do you store instead, and how does the user still recognise which card paid?
One balance is in a currency with exponent 3 and another with exponent 0. How do you store both exactly, and where does the exponent live?
A flag on the instrument row says which source is preferred now. How do you answer "which was preferred on the 5th", and what stops two sources being flagged at once?
A hold of {{hold_days}} days is released early by the review. Which rows does the release write, and what is the available balance at a moment between the two?
Where is the rate stored, and how do you prove later that the converted leg used the rate the user was shown?

incidents: The daily funding mix showed shares adding up to more than 100%: a payment funded partly by balance and partly by a card was counted once under each source instead of by leg amount.
Available balances in one currency went negative for a few seconds on busy days: two payment debits read a cached balance, and both passed the check before either was written.

With balances in up to {{currencies}} currencies, a monthly statement total was converted with today's rates rather than the rates applied at the time, so users saw last month's total change every day.

templates.title: Payment requests and splits as data — requests, partial payments, reminders, declines, group splits and each request's settled state as of a date
templates.subtopic: request and share lifecycles as events, reproducible split rounding, state as of a date, reminder eligibility

sections.scenario: Users ask other people for money: a request to one person, or a split of a bill among up to {{max_participants}} participants. There are about {{requests_per_day}} requests a day. In this exercise's rules (check current docs): a participant can pay their share in full or in several parts, decline it, or ignore it; the requester can cancel the request, or edit its amount until anyone has paid; a reminder goes out {{reminder_days}} days after the request to every participant who still owes something; an unpaid share expires after {{expiry_days}} days. A split divides the total equally by default, with leftover cents assigned by a stated rule, or by custom amounts the requester types. The requester's screen shows, per participant, what is paid and what is outstanding; analytics asks how many requests are settled within N days, per amount band, and what share of split shares are declined.
sections.problem: Design the data model for requests and splits. Cover requests (to one person or a group); the share each participant owes and how it was computed; payments made against a share (partial, several, possibly from a wallet in another currency); declines, cancellations and edits; reminders sent; expiry; and the state of each share and each request as of any date. Show how you answer: what each participant owed and had paid on date D; requests settled within N days, per week; and which participants are due a reminder today.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer minor units. The shares of a split add up exactly to the total; in this exercise's remainder rule, leftover minor units go one each to participants in the order they were added. A payment never exceeds what is outstanding on its share (an overpayment is rejected in this exercise). A request has one currency; a payment from a balance in another currency is converted once at the payer's quoted rate and recorded in the request's currency as well. Every change is an event: an edited request keeps its first amount in history. People see only requests they are part of; analytics see aggregates and amount bands, never who owes whom.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, participant limits and the reminder and expiry periods are hypothetical. Notification delivery is out of scope beyond recording that a reminder was sent. How participants without an account are identified is covered in another exercise; here a share may point at an invited identifier.
sections.criteria: Requests, shares and share events kept separate; shares that add up exactly under a stated, reproducible remainder rule; partial payments and declines as events; edits as versions; state as of any date derived by folding events; reminder eligibility per share, idempotent per share and day; rule versions recorded on each request; conversion recorded once; analytics in aggregates and amount bands; incidents explained and repaired from events.

clarifications.q: Is a request's state stored or derived?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but "state on date D" must be answerable for any past D.

clarifications.q: Can one payment answer two requests?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise a payment answers exactly one share; a participant with two shares pays twice.

clarifications.q: What happens when the requester edits the total?
clarifications.a: Allowed only before any payment; the edit recomputes the shares and is recorded as a new version of the request.

clarifications.q: Does a decline end the share?
clarifications.a: Yes. The share closes as declined, and the requester can send a new request.

clarifications.q: In which time zone is "{{reminder_days}} days after the request" counted?
clarifications.a: As {{reminder_days}} × 24 hours from the moment the request was created, sent at the next morning in the participant's own time zone (this exercise's rule).

hints: Request → shares (one per participant) → share events (paid, declined, expired, cancelled, reminded). A state is a fold of events up to a moment.
Keep how the shares were computed (the rule version, the total, the participants in order) so the split can be reproduced exactly.
"As of D" filters events by time and folds them; a daily snapshot of open shares is an optimisation, never the source of truth.
followups: Write out the shares for 100.00 split among three participants under this exercise's remainder rule, and the invariant you check on every split.
A participant pays 10.00 of a 33.34 share on Monday and 23.34 on Thursday. Which rows exist, and what does the requester see on Wednesday?
Write the query for "participants to remind today". How do you avoid reminding someone who paid an hour ago, or reminding twice after a retry?
Define "settled within N days" for a split in which one participant declined. Is the request settled, and what is the weekly metric's denominator?
At {{requests_per_day}} requests a day with splits of up to {{max_participants}} participants, what is the grain of the analytics fact, and how do you keep "state as of D" cheap?

rules.ask: One status per request: two of five participants paid, one declined. What does it say, and how do you remind only the two who still owe?
100.00 split three ways: which participant pays the extra cent, where is that recorded, and can the shares ever add up to 99.99?
A payment recorded late belongs before yesterday's snapshot. How is yesterday's state corrected, and what did the reminder job see?
The expiry rule changed from {{expiry_days}} days last month. Which rule does a request created before the change follow, and where is that recorded?
Reminders are due {{reminder_days}} days after creation, sent in each participant's morning. What does your job select, and what stops a second reminder after a retry?

incidents: A split among many participants showed shares adding up to one cent less than the bill: each share was rounded on its own and the remainder rule was never applied.
Reminders went to participants who had already paid: the reminder job read the request's status, which changed only when every share was settled.

After the expiry rule changed, last quarter's "expired requests" report changed too: expiry was computed at query time with the current {{expiry_days}}-day rule instead of the rule recorded on each request.

templates.title: Recipients by email, phone or username as data — identifiers that change hands, verification, payments to unclaimed identifiers and claim windows
templates.subtopic: identifiers as entities, holdings over time, resolution at send time, unclaimed-payment lifecycle with a stored deadline, pseudonymised analytics

sections.scenario: Users send money to an email address, a phone number or a username rather than to an account number. One account can hold several identifiers, and there are about {{identifiers}} identifiers in all. Identifiers change hands: carriers reassign phone numbers, people give up email addresses, and usernames are changed and later taken by someone else. In this exercise's rules (check current docs): an identifier receives money only while it is verified by its holder; a released username can be taken by another account only after {{quarantine_days}} days; a phone number whose verification lapses is detached until it is verified again. A payment sent to an identifier that no account holds waits as an unclaimed payment: the recipient has {{claim_window_days}} days to sign up and verify it, otherwise the money returns to the sender. About {{unclaimed_per_day}} payments a day go to unclaimed identifiers.
sections.problem: Design the data model for identifiers and the payments sent to them. Cover identifiers (normalised email, phone number in an international format, username) as entities of their own; each account's holding of an identifier over time, with verification events; username history; the recipient of a payment as entered, as resolved at send time, and as finally credited; unclaimed payments and their lifecycle (waiting, claimed, returned, cancelled by the sender) with a deadline; and the analytics: the share of unclaimed payments claimed within the window, time to claim, and returns per day. Show how you answer "which account held this phone number on date D" and "which account was credited for payment X, and why".
sections.constraints: An identifier has at most one verified holder at a time, and its history is never overwritten. Identifiers are personal data: analytics hold a surrogate or a keyed pseudonym, never the raw email address or number; a user sees their own identifiers and payments. The claim deadline is fixed when the payment is sent, from the rule then in force. The sender's money for an unclaimed payment is set aside when it is sent and either credited to the claimant or returned. Money is stored in integer minor units.
sections.assumptions: Identifier counts, volumes, the claim window and the quarantine are hypothetical. Verification is described generally (a code or a link confirmed by the holder); how carriers report reassigned numbers is out of scope beyond an event that may arrive late or never.
sections.criteria: Identifiers as entities with normalisation; holdings over time with verification and end reasons, at most one verified holder at a time; usernames with history and the quarantine rule; the recipient as entered, as resolved and as credited, stored on the payment; unclaimed payments as a state machine with a stored deadline and exactly-once returns; keyed pseudonyms in analytics; erasure that keeps payments reconcilable; incidents explained by the model and repaired from events.

clarifications.q: Are Alice@Example.com and alice@example.com the same identifier?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes: emails are matched case-insensitively. Say how you normalise phone numbers.

clarifications.q: Can the sender cancel an unclaimed payment?
clarifications.a: Yes, until it is claimed.

clarifications.q: A payment was resolved to an account at send time, and the identifier changed hands a minute later. Who gets the money?
clarifications.a: The account resolved at send time; the payment records it.

clarifications.q: How is the claim window counted?
clarifications.a: As {{claim_window_days}} × 24 hours from the moment the payment was sent; the deadline is stored on the payment.

clarifications.q: Can a username be reused at once?
clarifications.a: No. Only after the {{quarantine_days}}-day quarantine in this exercise.

hints: An identifier is not a column on the user: it is an entity with holdings (identifier, account, from, to, verified at, end reason).
Resolve the recipient once, at send time, and store the result on the payment; never resolve it again when reading.
An unclaimed payment is a small state machine with a deadline stored at creation; returns are driven by the stored deadline.
followups: Write the query: which account held phone number N on date D, and was the holding verified at that moment?
A carrier reassigns a number. The old holder's verification lapses on the 1st; the new holder verifies on the 20th. A payment to the number on the 10th: what happens, and which rows exist?
At {{unclaimed_per_day}} unclaimed payments a day, how does the return job find expired payments, and what makes each return happen exactly once?
Analytics asks for the share of new accounts created to claim a payment. Which tables answer it, and how do you avoid joining to each identifier's current holder?
A user asks to close their account and erase their data. Which identifier rows are kept, erased or pseudonymised, and how do past payments still reconcile?

rules.ask: A carrier reassigns a number to someone new. With the number stored on the user row, what does "who held it on the 10th" return?
Last quarter's report of payments received by new accounts changed this week. What did your join do when identifiers changed hands?
Is a plain hash of a phone number enough to keep it out of analytics? What would you use instead, and who holds the key?
The claim window changed from {{claim_window_days}} days. Which deadline does a payment sent the day before the change keep, and where is it recorded?
How do you enforce "one verified holder at a time" with history kept, when two accounts verify the same email address within the same second?

incidents: A payment to a reassigned phone number reached the previous holder's account: their holding row had no end, because the lapse of their verification was never written as an event.

Unclaimed payments were returned up to a day early for some senders: the return job compared the send date plus {{claim_window_days}} days with today's date in UTC instead of the deadline instant stored on the payment.
A report of payments received by new accounts changed after a wave of username changes: it joined payments to each identifier's current holder instead of the account credited at the time.

templates.title: Buyer protection claims as data, from the buyer's side — the purchase, the claim, messages and evidence, escalation, the decision, refunds and versioned programme rules
templates.subtopic: claim lifecycle as events, messages and evidence with visibility and retention, rule versions fixed at opening, refunds against funding legs

sections.scenario: A buyer who paid a merchant through the wallet can open a claim when an item did not arrive or arrived significantly not as described. There are about {{claims_per_day}} claims a day. In this exercise's programme rules (check current docs): a claim must be opened within {{claim_window_days}} days of the purchase; the buyer and the seller first exchange messages; the seller has {{seller_response_days}} days to respond, after which the buyer can escalate the claim to a review; the reviewer decides in the buyer's favour, in the seller's favour, or for a partial refund; and a refund is issued in the purchase currency. The rules change over time: the window, the eligible categories and the evidence asked for are versioned. The buyer sees their claim's timeline; the programme team sees aggregates.
sections.problem: Design the data model for claims from the buyer's side. Cover the purchase as the buyer sees it (merchant, amount, currency, items, shipment tracking references); the claim, its reason and the items and amount claimed; the claim's lifecycle as events (opened, message, seller responded, escalated, information requested, decided, refunded, closed, reopened); messages between buyer and seller with their attachments; evidence with its type, storage reference, who may see it, and retention; the decision with its outcome, amount, reason codes and rule version; refunds and their link to how the purchase was funded; and versioned programme rules. Show how you answer: the claim's timeline as the buyer sees it; time from opening to decision per category and month; the share of claims escalated; and which rule version governed claim X.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer minor units, with each currency's exponent from reference data. Refunds on a purchase never add up to more than the purchase amount. The rule version is fixed when a claim is opened (this exercise's rule). A decision records an outcome and reason codes about the transaction, never a judgement about a person's honesty or creditworthiness. Evidence files live in an object store; the model holds references and access rules. A seller never sees the buyer's other claims or account details. Evidence is kept for {{evidence_retention_years}} years after the claim closes and then deleted, while the claim's facts remain.
sections.assumptions: Claim volumes, the window, the seller deadline and retention are hypothetical. Card-network disputes are out of scope: a claim here is opened with the wallet provider. How a reviewer reaches a decision is out of scope; the model records it.
sections.criteria: The purchase as the buyer sees it; claims with append-only events and derived state and durations; messages and evidence with per-party visibility, storage references and retention; decisions with outcome, amount, reason codes and rule version, no judgements about people; refunds capped by the purchase and tied to the funding legs; rule versions fixed at opening; aggregates for the programme team; incidents explained and repaired without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Can a claim cover part of an order?
clarifications.a: Yes. The claim names the items and the amount claimed.

clarifications.q: Who can see an attachment?
clarifications.a: The buyer and the reviewer always; the seller only when the buyer attaches it to a message to the seller (this exercise's rule).

clarifications.q: Can a closed claim be reopened?
clarifications.a: Yes, once, within 10 days of the decision in this exercise. It keeps its id and its rule version.

clarifications.q: How is the seller's deadline counted?
clarifications.a: As {{seller_response_days}} × 24 hours from the moment the claim was opened.

clarifications.q: Does a refund go back to a card or to the balance?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, to the sources that funded the purchase, in the reverse order they were used.

hints: A claim header plus append-only claim events; the current state and every duration are derived from them.
Evidence is metadata rows with visibility and a retention date; the files are elsewhere.
Programme rules as versioned rows; the claim stores the version it was opened under.
followups: Write the query for the buyer's timeline of one claim, with the messages and the evidence the buyer may see.
Define time to decision for a claim that is reopened and decided twice. Which decision counts in the monthly report?
The window changes from {{claim_window_days}} days on the 1st. A purchase made before the change, a claim opened after it: which window applies, and what does the buyer see if the claim is too late?
A partial refund of 30% on a purchase funded by balance and a card: which rows are written, in which currency, and how is the amount rounded?
After {{evidence_retention_years}} years, evidence files are deleted. What remains, and how do the reports and the timeline still work?

rules.ask: The monthly report needs time from opening to decision and the share escalated. With one status column overwritten, which timestamps are left?
