The window changed last month. How does a claim opened today, for a purchase made before the change, find its rule version, and where is that stored?
The seller may see an attachment only if the buyer sent it to them. Where is that rule stored, and how do you serve the file to the seller without exposing the buyer's other files?
Two partial refunds on one purchase, the second after a reopening. What stops the total exceeding the purchase amount, and where is the currency's exponent applied?
Evidence is deleted after {{evidence_retention_years}} years. What happens to the decision, the reports and a message that referenced the file?

incidents: After the window changed from {{claim_window_days}} days, claims already open were re-evaluated against the new window, and some buyers saw "not eligible" on claims that had been accepted when they were opened.
Partial refunds in a currency with exponent 0 were issued 100 times too large: the amount was computed in major units and converted with an assumed exponent of 2.
Buyers could not escalate for days in one month: the {{seller_response_days}}-day seller deadline was computed from the seller's first reading of the claim instead of from its opening.

templates.title: Late claims — buyer protection claims filed after this exercise's window, per item category and month, reopened claims counted once
templates.subtopic: rule in force on a date, calendar dates in the buyer's time zone, inclusive windows, reopenings counted once, median

sections.scenario: A buyer who paid through the wallet can open a buyer protection claim on a purchase. In this exercise a claim is on time when it is filed within the window in force on the purchase date; programme_rules holds the window's versions (this exercise's rule; check current docs for how a real programme works). A closed claim can be reopened: a reopening is a new row in claims whose reopens_claim_id points at the row it reopens. The programme team wants a monthly view, per item category, of how many claims arrive after the window and how long buyers take to file. {{rule_rule}} {{tz_rule}} The sample has {{purchase_count}} purchases and {{claim_rows}} claim rows, {{reopen_rows}} of them reopenings.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns item_category, claim_month, claims, late_claims, reopened_claims, median_days_to_claim, one row per item category and month with at least one claim, ordered by item_category, claim_month.

  • A claim is a row with reopens_claim_id IS NULL (an original claim). A reopening is never a claim of its own, and a claim's dates are always its original filing's. {{chain_rule}}
  • Dates are calendar dates in the buyer's time zone (buyers.time_zone): the purchase date from purchased_at, the filing date from the original claim's filed_at. claim_month is the filing date's month as text, 'YYYY-MM'.
  • days_to_claim is the filing date minus the purchase date, in days. The window is the window_days of the programme_rules row with the latest effective_from on or before the purchase date. A claim is late when days_to_claim is greater than the window, so a claim filed on the window's last day is on time.
  • claims counts the group's claims, late_claims the late ones, and reopened_claims those that some row reopens directly.
  • median_days_to_claim is the median of the group's days_to_claim (percentile_cont(0.5): the mean of the two middle values when the count is even).
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). purchased_at and filed_at are TIMESTAMPTZ and the session runs in UTC. The sample's time zones have no daylight-saving changes, but the query should not rely on that. amount_minor and currency are shown for context and play no part. Production has hundreds of thousands of claims a day; the report runs monthly and is restated when late events arrive.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, buyers, categories, windows and dates. The window and its versions are this exercise's rules, not any real programme's. Lateness here is a reporting fact about timing, not a decision about any claim or any buyer.
sections.criteria: Original claims counted once, with dates from the original filing; reopenings used only for reopened_claims, matched by the row they reopen; dates in the buyer's time zone with integer date subtraction; the rule in force on the purchase date, inclusive of its effective_from; a strictly-greater lateness test; a correct median; deterministic order; can discuss category-specific rules, restatements and indexing.

clarifications.q: Is a claim filed exactly window_days after the purchase late?
clarifications.a: No. Late means strictly more days than the window.

clarifications.q: Which rule applies to a purchase made before a rule change and claimed after it?
clarifications.a: The rule in force on the purchase date, taken in the buyer's time zone.

clarifications.q: Which month does a claim reopened the following month belong to?
clarifications.a: The month of its original filing; it is counted once, there.

clarifications.q: Should I count 24-hour periods?
clarifications.a: No. Count calendar dates in the buyer's time zone: bought at 23:00 on the 1st and filed at 01:00 on the 3rd is 2 days.

clarifications.q: What if a category has no claims in a month?
clarifications.a: Leave the row out.

hints: Start from original claims only. Reopenings matter only for reopened_claims: EXISTS a row whose reopens_claim_id is the claim's id.
(ts AT TIME ZONE b.time_zone)::date is the buyer's local date, and subtracting two dates gives an integer number of days.
The rule in force on a date is a "latest row on or before" lookup: a LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1, or validity ranges built with LEAD(effective_from).
followups: The programme later sets a shorter window for one category. How do programme_rules and the lookup change?
The report is restated monthly. A reopening arrives late, or a buyer's time zone is corrected. Which months change, and how would you materialise the report so a restatement is cheap?
At production volume, how would you index claims and programme_rules for this query, and would you store the local purchase date?
The team wants late claims broken down by days late (1–7, 8–30, more than 30). Extend the query and say what the denominator of a late share is.

rules.ask: One purchase can carry more than one original claim. What does counting distinct purchases do then, and what unit should you count?
COALESCE(reopens_claim_id, claim_id) climbs one level. What happens to a reopening of a reopening?
Is 23:00 on the 1st to 01:00 on the 3rd one day or two in this report, and what does your expression return?
Which time zone's date does filed_at::date give in this session, and which claims change month or lateness because of it?
Show the comparison you use for lateness. Is a claim filed on the window's last day late in your query?
Which rule version applies to a purchase made before the last change: the one in force on the purchase date, or simply the newest?

incidents: One month's late share doubled after a release of the claims app: reopenings were written as new claims without reopens_claim_id, so each one counted as a claim filed weeks after its purchase.

For months, buyers in time zones ahead of UTC were reported late more often than others: the report took dates in UTC, so a purchase made early in the buyer's morning moved to the previous date, and claims filed on the window's last local day counted as late.
A window version loaded ahead of its effective date was applied at once to every claim: the lookup took the newest version instead of the one in force on the purchase date.

templates.title: A social payments feed with privacy — audiences, retroactive changes, blocks and hidden payments that never resurface
templates.subtopic: audience rules, retroactive visibility changes, read-time enforcement

sections.scenario: A peer-to-peer payments app with about {{users}} active users shows a social feed: when two people pay each other, the payment can appear to others with the participants' names, the note they wrote and the time, but never the amount (this exercise's rule). About {{payments_per_day}} payments a day are made, and a typical user has around {{friends}} friends, with some accounts far above that. Each payment is posted with an audience: public, friends or private. Under this exercise's rule (check current docs), a user has a default audience that applies to new payments unless they override it on the payment; a payment is shown with the most restrictive audience chosen by any of its participants; a participant can later make a past payment more private, one at a time or all at once, but never less private. A user can block another, after which neither sees the other's payments anywhere, including ones made before the block. A participant can hide a payment from the feed, and a note can be removed after a report; neither may ever be seen again by anyone it was hidden from.
sections.problem: Design the feed. Cover the write path from a completed payment to feed entries; how the effective audience is computed and stored; fan-out to friends' feeds versus assembling feeds on read, and what you do for accounts with very large friend lists; the read path and where privacy is enforced; how a retroactive change (one payment made private, or all past payments at once), a block, or a hide takes effect everywhere within {{propagation}}; caches, search, notifications and rebuilds; and how you would prove continuously that nothing hidden is being served.
sections.constraints: A feed page loads in under 300 ms at p99. A privacy change, a block or a hide takes effect on every surface within {{propagation}}, and a stale copy must fail closed: if the system is unsure whether a viewer may see an entry, it does not show it. The amount of a payment never enters the feed path. People see only what their audience allows; no analytics on the feed identifies an individual's payments outside that person's own view.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, times and rules are hypothetical. The payments system is given: it emits a completed-payment event with the payment id, participants, note, time and each participant's chosen audience. The friend graph is a given service with friend lists and a change stream. A trust and safety team decides note removals; you receive the decisions.
sections.criteria: Separates immutable payment facts from a versioned visibility record (effective audience as the most restrictive participant choice, hides, removals, blocks); a fan-out strategy justified with numbers for {{payments_per_day}} payments and about {{friends}} friends, with a different path for very large friend lists; privacy enforced at read time on every surface (feed, profile, search, notifications, exports), failing closed when the visibility version is uncertain, so retroactive changes take effect within {{propagation}} without rewriting every copy; tombstones and visibility versions that rebuilds, snapshots and replays must honour; continuous verification (sampled re-checks of served entries against the visibility store, canary viewers) and audit; amounts kept out of the feed path; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: If I pay a friend and my default is public but theirs is friends-only, what does the feed show?
clarifications.a: Friends-only, under this exercise's rule: the most restrictive participant choice wins. Whose friends see it is yours to define; say what you chose.

clarifications.q: Can a payment ever become more public later?
clarifications.a: No. Past payments can only become more private in this exercise.

clarifications.q: Does a new friendship show the new friend old friends-only payments?
clarifications.a: Your call; say what you choose and why. Ending a friendship must remove them from view within {{propagation}}.

clarifications.q: Are there other surfaces besides the home feed?
clarifications.a: Yes: each user's profile list, search over notes, notifications, and a data export of a user's own activity.

clarifications.q: Does the feed have to be in exact time order?
clarifications.a: Newest first by payment time; a few seconds of disorder between entries is acceptable.

hints: Separate what a payment is (immutable facts) from who may see it (a small, mutable visibility record). Fan-out copies can carry the first; the second must be checked on read.
Fan-out on write is cheap to read and expensive to change; fan-out on read is the opposite. A hybrid, with a different path for accounts with very large friend lists, is common.
Treat every privacy change as an event with a version. A copy of an entry is servable only if it has been checked against a visibility version at least as new as the latest change.
followups: Walk through one payment from completion to appearing in a friend's feed. Which records are written, and which of them change when a participant later makes it private?
A user with 40,000 past payments makes them all private at once. How does that take effect within {{propagation}} without rewriting 40,000 times their friend count feed entries?
A block is applied. Which surfaces must change, in what order, and what does the blocked person's next feed request see?
A region fails over and feed caches are rebuilt from a snapshot taken two hours earlier. How do you guarantee that nothing hidden in those two hours comes back?
How would you detect, continuously and in production, that an entry is being shown to someone its audience excludes?

rules.ask: An account with 5,000 friends sets all past payments to private. How many feed entries are now wrong, and what is served in the meantime?
A feed request now needs a few hundred friends' recent payments and a visibility check for each. What is the p99, and what do you cache?
The cache holds a rendered page that includes a payment hidden a minute ago. What makes that page unservable?
A rebuild job reads the payments table, which still has the hidden payment. What stops the job from putting it back into feeds?
Which privacy changes are you willing to make eventual, and how does the read path fail closed while they propagate?

incidents: A user makes all 30,000 of their past payments private. The change queue processes it in batches behind other work, and six hours later some of those payments are still in friends' feeds, far beyond the {{propagation}} target.

After a regional failover, feed caches are rebuilt from a snapshot taken two hours before. Payments that were hidden, and notes that were removed, during those two hours reappear for about 20 minutes.
A new release of the feed service computes the audience from the payer's setting only. For three hours, payments whose recipient had chosen friends-only are shown publicly.
A block is applied correctly to the home feed, but the blocked person still finds the blocker's past payments through note search, which is served by a separate index refreshed hourly.

templates.title: Pay-later reminders and autopay for consumers — notices, attempts across funding sources, retries and a schedule people can trust
templates.subtopic: local due dates, idempotent payment attempts, notifications, no credit conclusions

sections.scenario: A wallet offers consumers a pay-later option at checkout: a purchase is split into instalments due on set dates (for example four instalments two weeks apart; this exercise's rule, check current docs). About {{plans}} plans are active across {{markets}} markets and many time zones. Each instalment is due on a date in the consumer's own time zone. Autopay is on unless the consumer turns it off: on the due date the instalment is charged to the funding source the consumer chose for the plan; under this exercise's rule, another of their funding sources is tried only if they opted in to a fallback. A reminder goes out {{reminder_days}} days before each due date. A declined attempt is retried up to {{retries}} times on later days (this exercise's rule). Consumers can pay early in the app, pay part of an instalment, change the funding source, or turn autopay off at any moment, including minutes before it runs. Some funding sources, such as bank transfers, report success only days later and can be returned after that.
sections.problem: Design the reminder and autopay system. Cover the schedule store and how due dates are computed and kept in local time; the scheduler that finds what is due and runs it exactly once; the attempt workflow with fallbacks and retries; how a manual payment, a funding change or an autopay switch-off that arrives at the same moment as an autopay attempt is resolved; notifications (reminders, receipts, failure notices) that are timely, not duplicated and sent at sensible local hours; pending and returned bank payments; and the analytics that show whether reminders and autopay are working. The system draws no conclusion about any person's credit-worthiness or eligibility; it schedules, attempts, notifies and records.
sections.constraints: No instalment is ever charged twice, and no instalment that was already paid is charged at all. A consumer is never told an instalment is paid until it is, and never told it failed when it is still pending. Reminders and failure notices are sent between 08:00 and 21:00 local time. Every attempt, its funding source, the response and every notice is recorded with a reason. Analytics are aggregates (by market, funding type, attempt number); only a consumer sees their own schedule and history.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and rules are hypothetical. The payment service that charges a funding source is given and accepts a caller-supplied attempt id, so a repeated request with the same id returns the first outcome. Late-fee and hardship rules, if any, are decided by a separate service you call; you do not design them. A notification service is given and delivers push, email and text.
sections.criteria: Due dates as local calendar dates with the zone kept and run instants computed at scheduling time (daylight saving handled); a durable, partitioned schedule index (by due date and market) with catch-up after downtime; instalments as versioned state machines with conditional transitions shared by autopay and manual payment, reading from the primary; attempt ids for idempotency with the payment service; fallback only with consent and in the consumer's order; retries spread over time with jitter and capped at {{retries}}; pending and returned bank payments modelled explicitly, with honest notices; notifications deduplicated by (instalment, notice type) and held to local hours; aggregate analytics of reminder and attempt outcomes with no labels about people and no credit or eligibility conclusions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: At what time on the due date does autopay run?
clarifications.a: Your call, in the consumer's local time; say why. The instalment counts as on time if paid by the end of the due date locally.

clarifications.q: What if the consumer moves to another time zone?
clarifications.a: Due dates stay the same calendar dates; decide which zone governs when autopay runs, and say how you record the change.

clarifications.q: Are retries on the same funding source?
clarifications.a: First the plan's source; the fallback only if the consumer opted in, and only in the order they set. Retries happen on later days under this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Does the consumer see a failed attempt immediately?
clarifications.a: Yes, with what happens next. Pending bank transfers must be shown as pending, not as paid.

clarifications.q: Can analytics label consumers as risky or likely to miss payments?
clarifications.a: No. Report what happened to schedules and attempts in aggregate; no labels about people.

hints: Store due dates as local calendar dates plus the consumer's time zone; compute the run instant from them when scheduling, not once at plan creation.

Each instalment is a small state machine with a version. An attempt is allowed only if it wins a conditional transition (due → attempting) against the version it read; a manual payment uses the same transition.
An attempt id derived from (instalment, attempt number) makes a retried request harmless, because the payment service returns the first outcome.
followups: Walk through one instalment: reminder, due date, a declined first attempt, a successful retry on the fallback source. Which records and notices exist at the end?
A consumer pays the instalment manually at 08:59 and autopay is scheduled for 09:00. Show why your design cannot charge twice.
A bank transfer used by autopay is reported as returned three days after it was shown as pending. What changes in the schedule, and what is the consumer told?
How does the scheduler find a day's due instalments across {{markets}} markets without one huge scan, and what happens if it is down for six hours?
How do you measure whether reminders help, in aggregate, without drawing conclusions about individual consumers?

rules.ask: Your nightly job runs at one moment for every time zone. Whose due date is it at that moment, and who is charged on the wrong day?
The attempt message is delivered twice, two minutes apart, to two workers. What stops the second charge?
The due date is a local calendar date. What happens to a consumer's 09:00 autopay on the night clocks change?
A bank outage declines 200,000 attempts on one morning and every retry is scheduled for the same time tomorrow. What happens then?
The lock holder pauses for 40 seconds while holding the lock on an instalment. What does the manual payment path do meanwhile, and how do you avoid acting on an expired lock?

incidents: On the night clocks change in two of the {{markets}} markets, the scheduler computes run times from a fixed UTC offset stored at plan creation. Autopay runs a day early for about 60,000 instalments, and some consumers' accounts are overdrawn by a charge they expected the next day.
About 1,400 consumers who paid manually in the minutes before autopay were charged again, because the autopay worker read the schedule from a replica that was a few seconds behind.

A bank-transfer outage declines a large share of one morning's attempts. Every retry is queued for the same hour the next day, the payment service throttles, and failure notices go out to consumers whose transfers were in fact still pending.
A notification change ignores local time, and {{reminder_days}}-day reminders reach consumers in one market at 03:00.

templates.title: Checkout buttons on merchant sites, at the consumer-experience level — shown, clicked, signed in, funding chosen, completed, with no card details in analytics
templates.subtopic: funnel joins, SDK versions, data minimisation

sections.scenario: About {{merchants}} merchant websites and apps show a wallet checkout button. They integrate it in several ways: a hosted JavaScript SDK, mobile SDKs, server-side integrations that redirect the shopper, and plugins for e-commerce platforms; {{sdk_versions}} SDK versions are in use at once. Buttons are rendered about {{renders}} times a day. From the shopper's side the journey is: the button is shown, the shopper clicks it, signs in (or continues as a guest where allowed), chooses how to pay (wallet balance, bank, card or pay later), reviews and completes, or abandons, cancels or hits an error. Product teams want this funnel per integration type, SDK version, button configuration, platform and country, refreshed within {{freshness}}; each merchant should see its own funnel and no one else's. The payment itself and its outcome are recorded by the payments platform, which is given.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry and analytics: what the button and the checkout pages emit, how events from third-party pages are collected and validated, how client events are joined with server-side outcomes into one funnel per checkout session, how SDK versions and integration types are handled, the models and serving for internal teams and for each merchant, and how you guarantee that no card number, security code, bank account number or other payment credential ever reaches analytics.
sections.constraints: Analytics carry the funding category (balance, bank, card, pay later), never a card number, security code, expiry, bank account number or shopper contact detail. Merchants see only their own aggregates, with small counts suppressed. A shopper's checkout must never be slowed or broken by telemetry. Funnel numbers within {{freshness}} for dashboards; daily numbers final after 48 hours.
sections.assumptions: All volumes are hypothetical. Each checkout session has a session id issued when the button is clicked and recorded by the payments platform with the outcome; impressions happen before any session exists. Some shoppers block third-party scripts or telemetry endpoints, and some merchant pages restrict where scripts may send data. Bots load merchant pages.
sections.criteria: Clear event definitions (rendered versus visible, click, sign-in, funding category, outcome) with schema versions per SDK; collection that never blocks checkout (async, batched, sendBeacon-style), with an allowlist per schema version, no free text, and credential detection (checksum and pattern scanners) with quarantine and purge; impressions aggregated or sampled with known rates, clicks and sessions exact; a session-level funnel joining client events to authoritative server outcomes by session id, with explicit handling of missing client events; dedupe keys that survive retries and reloads; per-merchant aggregates with suppression and access scoped to the merchant; freshness within {{freshness}} for dashboards with late-data correction and final daily numbers; fair comparison of configurations; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: What counts as "shown"?
clarifications.a: Define it. Rendered in the page and rendered in the visible part of the screen are different numbers; say which you report and how you measure it.

clarifications.q: Can we use the shopper's email to join events?
clarifications.a: No. Use the session id and identifiers issued for telemetry only.

clarifications.q: Are server-side outcomes complete?
clarifications.a: Yes for completed, cancelled and declined sessions, minutes after they happen. Client events are lossy.

clarifications.q: Do merchants get raw events?
clarifications.a: No, aggregates of their own traffic only.

clarifications.q: Can a new SDK version change the events?
clarifications.a: Yes; event schemas are versioned and old SDKs stay in the wild for years.

hints: Trust the server for outcomes and the client for what happened before them. A funnel that divides server completions by client clicks needs a rule for sessions whose client events never arrived.
Allowlist fields at the collector, per schema version, and drop anything else; free text is where credentials leak.
Impressions are the largest stream and the least important per event: aggregate them early (or sample with a known rate) and keep clicks and sessions exact.
followups: Walk through one checkout from button shown to completed. Which events exist, which ids join them, and which record is authoritative for each step?
An SDK version starts sending "shown" twice whenever the cart updates. How do you detect it and correct the history?
On one merchant's site, completions appear with no clicks at all. What is happening, and how does your funnel avoid a conversion above 100%?
A scanner finds something shaped like a card number in raw event storage. Walk through the first hour and the following week.
How would you compare conversion between two button configurations fairly when merchants choose their own configuration?

rules.ask: A small merchant gets 300 renders a day. What does sampling do to its own funnel, and what do you show it?
Which identifier joins a shopper's events across sessions in your design, and do you need it at all for this funnel?
An SDK sends the browser's error message text as-is. What could be in it, and where do you stop it?
The same click arrives twice with different event ids because the SDK retried after a page reload. What is your dedupe key?
Which numbers truly need {{freshness}} freshness, and what do you lose by computing the rest daily?

incidents: An SDK release among the {{sdk_versions}} versions in use fires the "shown" event again on every cart update. The overall click rate drops by a fifth overnight and a product team starts rolling back an unrelated button change.
A large merchant tightens the rules on where its pages may send data, blocking the telemetry endpoint. Its dashboard shows thousands of completed checkouts a day with almost no clicks.
A security scan finds strings that pass a card-number checksum in raw events from one SDK version's error field, collected over nine days.
On the busiest shopping day, the funnel pipeline falls six hours behind, well outside {{freshness}}, and dashboards show conversion collapsing.

templates.title: Linking banks and cards — verification, expiries and replacements, failed links, and analytics on where linking fails
templates.subtopic: external providers, state machines, failure taxonomy analytics

sections.scenario: Wallet users add banks and cards as funding sources: about {{links_per_day}} link attempts a day across {{institutions}} banks and card issuers. Verification is done in a few general ways (this exercise's options; check current docs): for banks, an instant check through one of {{providers}} verification providers where the user signs in to their bank, or two small test deposits the user confirms within {{confirm_days}} days; for cards, a small authorization that is reversed. A risk score you are given decides whether a link needs an extra step. After linking, cards expire and are replaced, sometimes with an update from the card network and sometimes only when a payment fails; bank links can break when the bank changes something. Product teams want to know where linking fails (by step, method, institution, provider, platform and app version) and to steer users to a method that works when one is failing.
sections.problem: Design the linking system and its analytics. Cover the instrument model and its lifecycle (started, pending verification, verified, failed, expired, replaced, removed); the integration with verification providers and the payment network, including timeouts and late answers; test-deposit links that wait for days; card expiries and replacements, and what happens to plans and defaults that point at a replaced card; a failure-reason taxonomy that stays useful as providers and app versions change; the analytics on where linking fails; and the health signal that steers users away from a failing method.
sections.constraints: Card numbers, security codes and bank account numbers are held only by a given token vault; your systems and analytics see a vault token, the instrument type, the institution and, for the user's own screens, the last four digits. A link is never shown as verified unless it is. A user sees their own instruments and failure messages; analytics are aggregates. How someone might get around verification is out of scope; you record what happened.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and rules are hypothetical. Providers answer through an API and, for some outcomes, a later callback; answers can arrive after your timeout. Card network updates, where available, arrive as a daily file. The payment service reports declines with a reason code.
sections.criteria: Instruments as state machines driven by events (attempt id, provider raw answer, normalised reason) with the current state as a projection; vault tokens and a keyed fingerprint instead of numbers, with analytics on types, institutions and reasons only; timeouts and late provider answers reconciled deterministically, with retries that reuse the pending attempt rather than creating new instruments; test-deposit waits with expiry after {{confirm_days}} days reflected on every screen; card replacements applied from network updates to plans, defaults and scheduled payments, with the user asked when no update arrives; a two-layer failure taxonomy with versioned mappings and an alert on unmapped codes; linking health per (institution, method, provider) with minimum counts and hysteresis to steer users without flapping; the given risk score used without describing how verification could be avoided; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the same card be linked to two accounts?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule it can, subject to the given risk score. Say how you recognise it is the same card without seeing the number.

clarifications.q: What happens to a pay-later plan or a default funding source when a card is replaced?
clarifications.a: If the network sends an update, the replacement takes over; otherwise the user is asked. Decide what is shown meanwhile.

clarifications.q: Are provider failure codes consistent?
clarifications.a: No. Each provider has its own codes and they change.

clarifications.q: How quickly do teams need linking health?
clarifications.a: Within five minutes for steering users to another method; daily for product analysis.

clarifications.q: What if a provider answers after the user gave up?
clarifications.a: It happens. The late answer must be recorded and must not leave the instrument in a contradictory state.

hints: Model each instrument as a state machine whose transitions are events with the provider's raw answer, your normalised reason, and the attempt id; the current state is a projection.

Keep two layers of failure reason: the provider's raw code, versioned, and your stable taxonomy (user abandoned, credentials rejected, provider unavailable, institution unavailable, verification mismatch, declined, timed out). Map with a table that can change without losing history.
Measure linking health as a rate per (institution, method, provider) over a short window with a minimum count, so a small bank with three attempts does not trip it.
followups: Walk through a bank link by test deposits that the user confirms on day four. Which records exist, and in which states, along the way?
A provider answers "verified" two minutes after your timeout marked the attempt failed and the user started a second attempt. What is the final state, and what does the user see?
A large issuer replaces several hundred thousand cards over a week. How do plans, defaults and scheduled payments follow the replacements?
How do you decide that a method is failing for one institution and steer users to another, without flapping or hiding a method for everyone?
The share of failures reported as "other" doubles after an app release. How would your design have prevented that from going unnoticed?

rules.ask: Where exactly in your pipeline could a full number appear, and what proves it never does?
Two users link the same card. What does your identifier let analytics see, and what must it never let anyone reconstruct?
The answer arrives after the timeout. Which state wins, and how do you avoid telling the user two different things?
You switch an institution's links to a second provider. How do you know the second provider is actually better for that institution and not just less observed?
The rate of successful links rises after you steer users away from instant checks. Is linking better, or did you just move failures into test deposits that are never confirmed?

incidents: One of the {{providers}} verification providers degrades for a large bank. Instant checks for that bank fail for 45% of attempts instead of 8%, users retry repeatedly, and each retry leaves another pending instrument behind.

A large card issuer replaces several hundred thousand cards after a security event. Network updates arrive over a week, and in the meantime scheduled payments and pay-later instalments fail with "expired card".
An app release introduces new provider error codes that the mapping table does not know. They are all counted as "other", which grows to 40% of failures, and the linking-health signal goes quiet.
Test-deposit links that users never confirm pile up; after {{confirm_days}} days the expiry job removes them, but the users' screens still show them as "pending".

templates.title: Consumer rewards and cash back — earning rules, pending until the return window passes, redemption, expiry and a balance users can trust
templates.subtopic: earn lots with states, return windows, clawback, expiry in local time

sections.scenario: A wallet runs a rewards programme for about {{members}} members. Members earn cash back on eligible purchases paid with the wallet: a base rate by purchase category plus about {{offers}} time-limited merchant offers active at once (this exercise's rules; check current docs). Rewards are held in integer minor units of the member's currency. Under this exercise's rules, a reward stays pending until {{return_days}} days after the purchase, because a return or refund in that time reduces or cancels it; then it becomes available. Available rewards can be redeemed to the wallet balance or at checkout, and each reward expires {{expiry_months}} months after it became available, at the end of that day in the member's time zone. Redemptions use the rewards that expire soonest first. A refund after a reward is available claws it back from the available balance; under this exercise's rule the balance never goes below zero, and any remainder is offset against future rewards. Members see pending, available, soon-to-expire and history in the app, and finance needs the outstanding rewards liability every day.
sections.problem: Design the rewards system: how purchases and refunds arrive and which rule versions apply; how a reward is computed and rounded; the record of each reward and its states (pending, available, redeemed in part or whole, expired, clawed back); redemption and expiry; the balance and history the member sees; reconciliation with purchases, refunds and redemptions; the daily liability for finance; and how a wrong rule is corrected after the fact.
sections.constraints: Every reward amount is an integer in minor units, computed by one stated rounding rule at one step. The member's available balance, history and statement always agree, and every change to a balance is traceable to a purchase, refund, redemption, expiry or correction. A member sees only their own rewards; analytics and finance use aggregates. Purchases and refunds can arrive days late.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates and periods are hypothetical. Purchase and refund events come from the payments platform with a purchase id, amount in minor units, currency, merchant category and time; refunds reference the purchase. Merchant offers are configured by a given offers tool with start and end times and a funding share paid by the merchant.
sections.criteria: Rewards as lots with rule versions and states, and every change as an entry referencing a purchase, refund, redemption, expiry or correction, so balance, history and statement are projections of one record; integer minor units with one rounding rule (including partial refunds); late refunds handled by state (reduce pending, claw back available with this exercise's offset rule); expiry after {{expiry_months}} months in the member's time zone and enforced on read; redemption soonest-expiring first with a conditional, idempotent spend that cannot use a reward twice; daily liability computed from the same entries and reconciled with members' balances and with purchases and refunds; corrections as dated, visible entries under a new rule version; caches that cannot serve a balance the record contradicts at redemption; aggregates only outside a member's own view; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: How is a partial refund handled?
clarifications.a: The reward is reduced in proportion to the refunded amount, rounded by your stated rule; say which way and why.

clarifications.q: Do base rate and offer stack?
clarifications.a: Under this exercise's rule, yes, up to a cap per purchase; the cap is part of the rule version.

clarifications.q: Which time zone governs expiry?
clarifications.a: The member's at the moment of expiry; record it with the expiry.

clarifications.q: Can a rule change apply to past purchases?
clarifications.a: Only as a correction of an error, never silently, and the member sees a dated correction entry.

clarifications.q: Is the rewards balance money the member owns?
clarifications.a: Treat it as a liability the programme owes until redeemed or expired; finance needs it exact.

hints: Make each reward a lot with its own amount, rule version, state and dates; the balance is a sum over lots, and every change is an entry against a lot.
Late refunds are normal. The refund's purchase id finds the lot wherever it is; what happens depends on the lot's state at that moment.
Expiry is a date in the member's zone; compute "expires today" from the zone, and make an available lot past its expiry count as expired on read, even if the job that marks it has not run.
followups: Walk through one purchase with a base reward and an offer, a partial refund on day 20, and a redemption on day {{return_days}} plus one. Which entries exist at the end?
A merchant's refunds arrive 12 days late, after the rewards became available and some were redeemed. What happens to each member's balance?
How do you compute the daily liability for finance, and how do you prove it equals the sum of members' balances?
A rule error doubled cash back on one category for nine hours. How do you correct it, and what do members see?
How would you change the design to let members redeem at checkout with a sub-second answer that can never spend the same reward twice?

rules.ask: A 3% reward on a purchase of 1,999 minor units. What is the amount, where is it rounded, and does the partial refund round the same way?
The balance and the history disagree for one member. Which one is right, and how would you know?
The job that moves pending rewards to available stops for two days. What do members see, and is anything lost?
The cached balance shows a reward that a refund clawed back a minute ago, and the member redeems it. What happens?
You recompute every reward under the corrected rule. Which members see a change, and how is each change shown to them?

incidents: A large merchant's refund feed arrives 12 days late. The rewards on those purchases are already available, and some members have redeemed them; about 8,000 members would go below zero without this exercise's offset rule.
The expiry job runs at midnight UTC for everyone. Members in the Americas see rewards expire on the evening before the date shown in the app.
An offer configured with the wrong rate doubles cash back on one category for nine hours, creating about 400,000 rewards that are still pending within the {{return_days}}-day window.
After a cache was added in front of the balance, 0.3% of members see an available balance that differs from their history and statement.

templates.title: A partner's errors that your users experience as yours
templates.subtopic: evidence, user communication, influence without authority

partner: the bank-transfer provider used for withdrawals in one market
the provider that verifies linked bank accounts
the provider that delivers one-time sign-in codes by text message
symptom: withdrawals shown as sent arrive a day or more late
bank links fail with a generic error and users retry again and again
sign-in codes arrive minutes late or not at all

sections.scenario: Your team owns the integration with {{partner}}. For {{weeks}} weeks, about {{share}} of the users who depend on it have found that {{symptom}}. Support contacts are rising, app-store reviews and public posts blame the wallet, and some users have stopped using the feature. The partner's own dashboard shows them meeting the service levels in their agreement. A partnerships manager owns the relationship and the agreement; your team owns the code that calls the partner, what the app shows while it waits, and the data about every request.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you establish, with evidence, where the failure is (your side, the partner's, or the boundary between them); what you can do for users now without waiting for the partner; what users are told, and by whom; how you work with the partnerships manager and the partner's engineers; what you change so the next problem is seen in hours rather than weeks; and when you would look for a second provider. Then tell me about a real time a dependency you did not control hurt your users, with what you did, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot change the partner's systems or the agreement. Public statements go through the communications team. You draw no legal conclusion about the agreement; that is for the partnerships and legal teams, and you bring them evidence.
sections.assumptions: The situation, figures and partner are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Establishes the facts first with end-to-end measurement split at the boundary, and is open to the problem being on their own side; acts now on what they control (honest in-app status and timing, retry and timeout behaviour that does not add load, support guidance) and measures harm, not only complaints; brings specific evidence (by market, bank, hour) to the partnerships manager and the partner's engineers, proposing a measure that reflects users' experience; communicates to users through the proper owners, honestly and without blaming by name; builds lasting detection (per-dependency service-level objectives on the user's outcome, joint dashboards, alerts) and decides on a second provider with evidence; draws no legal conclusions; real example with personal contribution and changed practice, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do we log every request to the partner?
clarifications.a: Yes, with timing and the partner's response code, but nobody has looked at them by market, bank or hour.

clarifications.q: Has the partner been told?
clarifications.a: Support has opened tickets; the partner answered that everything is within the agreed levels.

clarifications.q: Is there a second provider?
clarifications.a: Not today. Adding one would take at least a quarter.

clarifications.q: Can we tell users the partner is at fault?
clarifications.a: Not by name, and not without communications; you can tell them what is happening and what to expect.

hints: Measure the user's experience end to end, then split it at the boundary: time in your systems, time waiting for the partner, and what came back.
The agreement measures what it measures. Find the gap between it and what users experience; that gap is usually the conversation to have.
Some of the harm is in how the app behaves while it waits: honest status, sensible retries and clear timing expectations are yours to fix today.
followups: What would you look at in the first day, and what result would tell you the problem is on your side after all?
Your data shows the partner fails mostly for three banks and mostly at month end. How do you present that to the partner so they act on it?
What do you change in the app this week, and how do you know it reduced the harm rather than just the complaints?
The partner fixes it, then it recurs two months later. What should already be in place by then?
In your real example, what did you get wrong first, and what changed in how you manage dependencies?

rules.ask: The partner meets the agreed levels on paper. What measure would capture what users experience, and how would you get the partner to accept it?
Your retries double the load on a partner that is already struggling. How do you decide how many, and when to stop?
That takes a quarter and has its own risks. What do users get in the meantime, and what evidence would justify the switch?
To whom, with what, and what do you want them to decide?
What did you personally do or say, and when?

templates.title: Using customer support contacts to find and fix the biggest source of user confusion
templates.subtopic: measurement, privacy, cross-team prioritisation

data_state: contact reasons picked by agents from a list of 200, used inconsistently
free-text chat and email only, with no reason codes
reason codes from a list that was replaced three months ago, plus free text
candidates: money shown as pending versus available after a transfer
payments sent to an email or phone number that the recipient has not claimed
the amount a recipient abroad receives compared with what the sender expected

sections.scenario: The wallet's support teams handle about {{contacts}} contacts a week. The data you have is {{data_state}}. Product leaders each believe they know the biggest source of confusion; the loudest view is that it is {{candidates}}. You have been asked to find out what actually drives the most contacts that a product change could prevent, and to lead the fix with the product teams over the next {{weeks}} weeks.
sections.problem: How would you approach it? Cover how you turn the contact data into a trustworthy ranking of causes, with honest uncertainty; how you handle the personal information in contacts; how you choose what to fix (volume, harm to users, cost per contact, how fixable it is); how you get the owning product team to take it on; how you will know the fix worked; and how you keep the ranking current afterwards. Then tell me about a real time you used operational data such as support contacts, incidents or logs to change what a team built, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Contacts contain names, contact details and descriptions of people's money; access is restricted and every use must fit the support data policy. You do not own the product teams' roadmaps. Support agents' time is limited; you can ask for a small change to how they record contacts, not a new process.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Builds a trustworthy ranking (a hand-labelled sample, measured agreement of reason codes or classifiers, uncertainty stated) instead of trusting raw codes; handles personal data within policy (minimum access, redaction, aggregates, approval before new processing); ranks by preventable harm normalised by usage, not volume alone; engages the owning team with evidence and an agreed success measure; measures the effect fairly (comparison against expected volume, staged rollout or a hold-out where appropriate); keeps the ranking current with a small, durable change to how contacts are recorded; treats the loud view fairly; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can I read individual contacts?
clarifications.a: A small sample, under the policy, by people with access; anything wider must be redacted or aggregated.

clarifications.q: Is contact volume the only cost?
clarifications.a: No. Some confusions also lead to users sending money to the wrong person or abandoning a payment.

clarifications.q: Do product teams track contacts today?
clarifications.a: Not systematically; they hear about the worst cases.

clarifications.q: Is the loudest view wrong?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet. It might be right.

hints: Build the ranking on a labelled sample first: read and code a few hundred contacts by hand (under the policy), then check how well reason codes or an automatic classifier agree with your labels before trusting them at scale.
Rank by preventable harm, not raw volume: contacts per thousand active users of the feature, repeat contacts, and money or trust at stake.
Agree with the owning team, before the change ships, what number should move and by how much.
followups: Given the data you have, how would you size the top causes, with confidence intervals, before trusting any automatic labels?
Your ranking says the loudest view is third, not first. How do you present that to the leader who holds it?
The fix is a wording change on one screen. How do you measure its effect on contacts when contact volume moves with seasons and releases?
An analyst proposes running a language model over all transcripts. What has to be true before you agree?
In your real example, what did the data change that opinion alone would not have?

rules.ask: How do you know its labels are right, and what personal data does it see, where, and under whose approval?
Who looks at it every week, and what decision does it change?
How does what users say compare with what the contacts show, and which do you trust when they disagree?
The fix is a help screen. Is it right to withhold it from a hold-out group, and for how long?
Which part did you personally do?

templates.title: Turning a vague executive goal into a measurable plan
templates.subtopic: metric definition, scoping, trade-offs, alignment

goal: "make splitting a bill with friends effortless"
"make people trust that their money is where we say it is"

sections.scenario: At a planning meeting, an executive sets a goal for your area: {{goal}}. There is no definition, no baseline and no target, but there is a deadline: show progress within {{quarters}} quarters. You lead a group of about {{team}} engineers and analysts whose systems touch the goal, alongside product managers and teams you do not lead. Several teams have already started describing their existing plans in the goal's words.
sections.problem: How do you turn the goal into a plan? Cover what you do to understand what the executive actually means; how you define the measures (one main measure, the ones that must not get worse, and how each is computed); how you set a baseline and a target; how you choose the few bets most likely to move the main measure, and what you stop doing to make room; how you get the other teams and the executive to agree; and how you report progress honestly, including when the measure does not move. Then tell me about a real time you turned an unclear goal into a concrete plan, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Your group's headcount is fixed. Every measure must be computable from data you can get within a month. Progress reports go to the executive monthly.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clarifies intent with the executive using a few sharp questions; defines a main measure precisely (population, events, computation) with guardrails, a measured baseline and a target with a rationale; chooses a few bets tied to the measure, with explicit trade-offs and things stopped; aligns teams through a shared, agreed definition rather than mandate, and treats renamed projects on evidence; reports honestly, including no movement, and adjusts; is honest about where changing what users are told is legitimate and where it is not; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can I go back to the executive with questions?
clarifications.a: Yes, once, for thirty minutes, in the next two weeks.

clarifications.q: Is there an existing measure close to the goal?
clarifications.a: Several, defined differently by different teams, none agreed.

clarifications.q: Can the goal be met by changing what users are told rather than what happens?
clarifications.a: Some of it, honestly; say where that line is.

clarifications.q: Do other teams have to adopt your measure?
clarifications.a: Only if they agree it is right; you cannot make them.

hints: Translate the goal into a moment in the user's journey you can observe: what would a user experience if the goal were met, and how would you count it?
Pair the main measure with guardrails that it could tempt people to worsen (accuracy, cost, failed payments, support contacts).
A plan with fewer, bigger bets that you can measure separately beats a long list that claims credit for everything.
followups: Give me a concrete definition of the main measure for {{goal}}: the population, the start and end events, and the computation.
What would you ask the executive in your thirty minutes, and what would change depending on the answers?
Two teams' existing projects have been renamed to fit the goal. How do you decide whether they stay in the plan?
After two months the main measure has not moved. What do you report, and what do you change?
In your real example, how did the definition you started with differ from the one you ended with, and why?

rules.ask: What would make that number go up while users' experience got worse, and which guardrail catches it?
How often can you measure it, how noisy is it, and what behavioural measure would you pair it with?
What did you take off it to make room, and who disagreed?
The baseline itself turns out to be computed differently by two teams. Which do you use, and how do you settle it?
Which call did you personally make, and who did you have to persuade?

templates.title: A smaller market's needs against the largest market's roadmap
templates.subtopic: platform generality, technical debt, stakeholder trade-offs

need: support for a currency with no minor unit, which breaks screens, rounding and reports that assume two decimal places
support for payments to phone numbers, which is how most people there pay each other, where the product assumes usernames
support for bank transfers as the main funding source, with results known only the next day, where the product assumes instant card results

sections.scenario: Your team owns a shared part of the wallet used in every market. A market that accounts for about {{share}} of users, and is growing fast, needs {{need}}. The market's team has worked around the gap for a year with local fixes that keep breaking. The largest market's product leaders have a committed roadmap for your team for the next {{quarters}} quarters, and they argue that their market's users and revenue should come first. Both sides have asked you to decide what your team does next.
sections.problem: How do you decide, and how do you carry the decision through? Cover what you find out about the size of the problem (users affected, failures, cost of the workarounds, risk); whether the need is really one market's or a flaw in a shared assumption that will hit others; the options (do it now, do part of it, let the market's team build it on your platform with your support, defer with a date); how you bring both sides to a decision and who makes it; and how you communicate it to the side that does not get what it asked for. Then tell me about a real time you had to weigh a smaller group's needs against a larger group's, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Your team's capacity is fixed for the {{quarters}}-quarter period. Any change to the shared component must keep every market working. You are not the final decider on cross-market priorities; a product director over both is.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Sizes the problem with evidence (users affected, incidents from workarounds, money at risk, support load) and checks whether it is a flawed shared assumption rather than a local feature; compares options on the same terms, including middle options (remove the assumption first, enable the market's own engineers with review); respects decision rights, prepares a fair written comparison for the director and makes a clear recommendation; communicates the decision with reasons and a plan for the side that lost (dates, mitigations, safety fixes); protects correctness in every market (tests, flags, staged rollout); real example with outcome, personal contribution and relationships, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the local workarounds dangerous?
clarifications.a: Some have caused incorrect statements and failed payments; none has lost money yet.

clarifications.q: Will other markets need the same thing?
clarifications.a: Two more planned launches would, according to their plans.

clarifications.q: Can the market's team contribute engineers?
clarifications.a: Two, for a quarter, if someone reviews their work.

clarifications.q: Is the largest market's roadmap negotiable?
clarifications.a: Partly; its leaders have said which two items are fixed.

hints: Check whether the need is a market feature or a wrong assumption in the shared component; the second is debt that grows with each launch.
Put both sides' costs in the same units: users affected, money at risk, support load, engineering time, and what delay costs each.
Look for options between all and nothing, such as removing the wrong assumption first and letting the market's team build the rest.
followups: What evidence would you gather in the first two weeks, and from whom?
How would you show the largest market's leaders that the shared assumption is their risk too, if it is?
The director decides for the largest market's roadmap. What do you do for the smaller market in the meantime?
You take the market's two engineers for a quarter. How do you make sure what they build is safe for every market?
In your real example, how did the people whose request lost react, and what did you do about it?

rules.ask: Revenue favours the largest market by design. What else belongs in the comparison, and how do you weigh it?
The workarounds have already caused incorrect statements and failed payments. At what point does that stop being the market's problem and become yours?
How much more does the general version cost than the specific one, and how do you stop it becoming a project that never ships?
What do you put in front of the director, and does each side agree it describes their position fairly?
What was your recommendation, and did you hold it when it was unpopular?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for consumer wallets and peer-to-peer payments across currencies
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, currencies and minor units, privacy of payments

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: amounts in currencies whose minor units have 0, 2 or 3 digits, converted at most once and rounded by one stated rule
privacy changes to past payments honoured on every surface within minutes
proof that every exchange rate applied equals the quote the user accepted
each user seeing their own activity, and everyone else seeing only aggregates
scale: tens of millions of people paying each other
transfers between more than a hundred countries
hundreds of millions of wallet payments a month

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a consumer wallet with peer-to-peer and cross-border payments, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The wallet setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example integer minor units with the currency's exponent carried as data and one conversion step rounded by a stated rule; a versioned visibility record checked on every read path with tombstones that rebuilds honour; quotes stored with ids and expiry and referenced by each conversion; per-user views scoped to the user and aggregates with minimum group sizes for everyone else); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a payments system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, follow one payment from one currency to another: which ids, amounts, currencies and visibility settings it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A currency with no minor unit and one with three both pass through your system. Where is the exponent stored, and where exactly is an amount rounded?
A user disputes the amount their recipient received. What record lets you show which rate was applied and that it matches what they were shown?
Who outside the user can see one person's payments in your design, and why?
